**Surat Yunus**

**Section on its revelation**

Atiyyah and Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is Meccan (*Makki*, revealed in Mecca), and al-Hasan and Ikrimah also said so. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that among it is a Medinan (*Madani*, revealed in Medina) verse, His saying: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus 40]. In another narration from Ibn Abbas: "It contains three Medinan verses, the first of which is His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ [Yunus 94], up to the end of three verses." Qatadah also said this. Muqatil said: "It is Meccan except for two verses: His saying ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ [Yunus 94] and the one after it [Yunus 94-95]." Some said: "It is Meccan except for two verses, which are His saying ﴿Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy﴾ and the one after it [Yunus 58-59]."

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾

As for His saying (*Alif Lam Ra*), Ibn Kathir read *Alif Lam Ra* with a fatha on the *ra*. Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisai read it spelled out as letters, with a kasra on the *ra*. We have already discussed in the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah what covers the explanation of this category. This expression has been singled out for six opinions:

First: its meaning is "I am Allah, the One who sees," narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

Second: "I am Allah, the Merciful," narrated by Ata from Ibn Abbas.

Third: that it is part of one of the names of Allah. Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Alif Lam Ra*, *Ha Mim* and *Nun* are letters of *al-Rahman*."

Fourth: that it is an oath which Allah swore by, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

Fifth: that it is one of the names of the Qur'an, said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Sixth: that it is a name of the surah, said by Ibn Zayd.

Regarding His saying *Tilka* ("these"), there are two views. One: it means *hadhihi* ("this"), said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas and preferred by Abu Ubaydah. Two: it is used in its original sense. Then within this there are three opinions.

First: the reference is to the earlier books, the Torah and the Gospel, said by Mujahid and Qatadah. So the meaning is: "These stories that you hear are those verses that were described in the Torah and the Gospel."

Second: the reference is to the verses that have already been mentioned from the Qur'an, said by al-Zajjaj.

Third: *Tilka* refers to *Alif Lam Ra* and its like from the letters of the alphabet, meaning: those letters with which the surahs begin are "the verses of the Book," because the Book is recited with them and its words return to them. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Abu Ubaydah said: *al-Hakim* ("the Wise") means *al-muhkam al-mubayyan al-muwadhdah* ("the firmly established, clarified and made clear"). The Arabs sometimes use the form *fa'il* in the sense of *muf'il*. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿With me is that which is ready﴾ [Qaf 23: 18], meaning *mu'add* ("prepared").

[p. 5] **His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it a wonder to the people that We have revealed to a man from among them...﴾**

The occasion of its revelation: when God Most High sent Muhammad (ﷺ), the disbelievers denied this and said, "God is greater than that His messenger should be a human being like Muhammad." So this verse was revealed. By "the people" here is meant the people of Makkah, and by "the man" is meant Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning of "from among them" is that they know his lineage. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. As for the alif (interrogative particle), it is for rebuke and denial. Ibn al-Anbari said: The argument against them, for their being astonished at the sending of Muhammad, is omitted here, and it is clarified in His saying: ﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32]. That is: just as We have made this difference clear to you through observation, do not deny God's preferring whom He wills with prophethood. He omitted it here relying on what He had made clear in another place. He said: It has also been said that they were astonished at the mention of resurrection and rising again, because warning and glad tidings are connected with them. Thus their reply in many places indicates that this is so, such as His saying: ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], and His saying: ﴿He who brought them into being the first time will give them life again﴾ [Ya-Sin: 79].

Regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿a sure standing (qadam sidq)﴾, there are seven opinions:

The first: it is the good reward for what they sent forward of their deeds. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Salih narrated from him that he said: "A righteous deed they come forward with."

The second: it is the happiness that preceded for them in the first Remembrance. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "A precedence of truth."

The third: it is a true intercessor, namely Muhammad (ﷺ), who will intercede for them on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: it is a true predecessor who went ahead of them in faith. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The fifth: it is a station of truth from which there is no removal. This was said by 'Ata'.

The sixth: that the "qadam al-sidq" is the elevated rank. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The seventh: that the "qadam" here is the calamity of the Muslims with their Prophet (ﷺ), and the reward from God that reaches them at their grief over his loss and their love for seeing him. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

If it is asked: why did He choose "qadam" (foot) here rather than "yad" (hand), when the Arabs use "yad" in the sense of favour?

The answer: "qadam" is mentioned here for advancement, because the custom is that the one who strives goes forward on his feet. The Arabs use it as a metaphor for a deed in which one is ahead and in which there is no lagging. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"You have a foot that people do not deny,
along with ancestral nobility that has risen above the sea."

If it is asked: what is the reason for attributing "qadam" to "sidq" (truth)?

The answer: this is praise of the "qadam," and whatever you attribute to "sidq" you have praised. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿Cause me to enter a sure entrance and cause me to exit a sure exit﴾ [al-Isra': 80], and His saying: ﴿In a seat of truth﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. In the speech there is an omitted element, its implied sense being: "We revealed to a man from among them, and when the revelation came to them, the disbelievers said, 'Indeed this is manifest magic.'"

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "la-sahir" (a sorcerer) with an alif. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "la-sihr" (magic) without an alif. Abu 'Ali said: The saying "that We revealed to a man from among them" has already preceded. So whoever says "sahir" means the man; and whoever says "sihr" means that which was revealed, i.e., "sihr": the thing you yourselves say is revelation is magic.

Al-Zajjaj said: When he warned them of resurrection and rising again, they said, "This is magic." He informed them that the One who created the heavens and the earth is able to resurrect them, by His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is God﴾, and its explanation has already preceded in (al-A'raf: 54).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾. Mujahid said: He decrees it. Others said: He commands it and executes it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: no one intercedes except with His permission. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: No mention of an intercessor has occurred before this, but those being addressed used to say, "The idols are our intercessors."

The second: the meaning is that there is no second with Him, taken from "shaf'" (pair), because no one was with Him, and then He created things. So His saying "except after His permission" means: after His command that creation should be, and it was. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him﴾. Muqatil said: Declare Him one. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: worship Him alone. His saying "tadhakkarun" (you may remember) means: you may take heed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾, meaning: your final destination on the Day of Resurrection. "The promise of Allah is true." Al-Zajjaj said: "The promise of Allah" is in the accusative on the meaning: Allah has promised you a promise, because His saying "To Him is your return" means the promise of returning. And "true" (haqqan) is in the accusative on the meaning: that is indeed true, truly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He originates the creation﴾. Most readers recited it with a kasra on the alif (inna). ʿAʾisha, Abu Razin, ʿIkrima, Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Aʿmash recited it with a fatha (anna). Al-Zajjaj said: whoever recited it with a kasra, it is on the basis of a new sentence (istiʾnaf); whoever recited it with a fatha, the meaning is: "To Him is your return, because He originates the creation." Muqatil said: He originates the creation when it was nothing, then He restores it after death. As for al-qist, it is justice (al-ʿadl).

If it is said: How did He specify the recompense of the believers with justice, when His recompense of the disbelievers is also just?

The answer: If He had gathered the two groups together in justice, it would not have become clear, in their state of being gathered, what painful punishment befalls the disbelievers and drinking from boiling water (hamim). So He separated them from the believers, to make clear what He recompenses them with, which is also just. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. As for al-hamim, it is hot water. Abu ʿUbayda said: everything hot is hamim.

[p. 9] Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance (ḍiyāʾ)﴾. Most readers recited *ḍiyāʾ* with one hamzah. Ibn Kathir recited *ḍiʾāʾ* with two hamzahs throughout the Qur'an, meaning "possessing radiance." *Wa-l-qamara nūran* ("and the moon a light") means "possessing light." *Wa-qaddarahu manāzila* means "He determined for it," with the preposition omitted. The meaning is: He prepared and facilitated for it stations (manāzil).

Al-Zajjaj said: The pronoun refers to "the moon," because it is the one that determines the years and the reckoning. It may also refer to both the sun and the moon, with one of them omitted for brevity.

Al-Farra' said: If you wish, you may make the determination of the stations specific to the moon, because the months are known by it. If you wish, you may make the determination apply to both, and mention only one of them, as in His saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (al-Tawbah 62).

Ibn Qutaybah said: The stations of the moon are twenty-eight, from the beginning of the month to the twenty-eighth night, after which it disappears. These stations are the stars to which the Arabs attributed the *anwā'* (seasonal rains with their risings and settings). Their names among them are: al-Shirṭān, al-Buṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haq'ah, al-Han'ah, al-Dhirā', al-Nathrah, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabhah, al-Zubrah, al-Ṣarfah, al-ʿAwwā', al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawlah, al-Naʿā'im, al-Balda, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiyah, Far' al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Far' al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar, and al-Rishā', which is the fish.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah did not create that except in truth﴾, meaning for the sake of truth, namely to manifest His craftsmanship and power and as evidence of His oneness. ﴿He details the signs﴾: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim recited *yufaṣṣilu* with a *yāʾ*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim recited *nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt* with a *nūn*. The meaning is: We make them clear. ﴿For a people who know﴾: they derive evidence from the indications of His power.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who fear Allah﴾. There are two views concerning this:
One: they fear association (shirk).
The second: they fear the punishment of Allah.
The meaning is: The signs are for one whose desire does not lead him to oppose the truth that has become clear to him.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: They do not fear resurrection. ﴿And are content with the worldly life﴾: they chose what is in it over the Hereafter. ﴿And are at rest therein﴾: they preferred it. Others said: They relied upon it, because they do not believe in the Hereafter. ﴿And those who are heedless of Our signs﴾: there are two views concerning this:
One: they are the signs of the Qur'an and Muḥammad (ﷺ), as said by Ibn ʿAbbās.
The second: what He mentioned at the beginning of the surah of His creation, as said by Muqātil.
As for His saying "heedless," Ibn ʿAbbās said: They are deniers. Others said: They are turning away. Ibn Zayd said: These are the disbelievers.

Allah the Exalted said: *Bi-mā kānū yaksibūn* ("for what they used to earn"). Muqātil said: from disbelief and denial.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their Lord guides them by their faith﴾. There are four views concerning this:
One: He guides them to Paradise as a reward for their faith.
The second: He makes for them a light by which they walk, because of their faith.
The third: He increases them in guidance because of their faith.
The fourth: He rewards them because of their faith.
As for guidance itself, it had already preceded for them.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾: meaning they flow before them, and they see them from above.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their call therein﴾, meaning their supplication. We have explained this at the beginning of (Al-A'raf 5).

Concerning the meaning of this supplication there are two views:
One: it is their asking for what they desire. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Whenever the people of Paradise desire something, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and what they desire comes to them. When they have eaten, they say: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." That is the last of their supplication. Ibn Jurayj said: When a bird passes by them and they desire it, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and the angel brings them what they desire and greets them, and they return his greeting. This is His saying: ﴿And their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾. When they have eaten, they praise their Lord. This is His saying: ﴿And the last of their call is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾
The second: when they wish to turn to Allah the Exalted in a supplication they make, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah." Qatādah said this.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾. There are three views concerning this:
One: it is a greeting from some of them to others, and the angels' greeting to them, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās.
The second: Allah the Exalted greets them with peace.
The third: the greeting means sovereignty, so the meaning is: their sovereignty therein is secure. Al-Māwardī mentioned both of these views.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the last of their call﴾, meaning their supplication and their saying: ﴿That "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ Abū Mijlaz, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Ibn Yaʿmar, Qatādah, and Yaʿqūb recited *anna al-ḥamda lillāh* with a shaddah on the *nūn* and a fatḥah on the *dāl*. Al-Zajjāj said: Allah informed that they begin with the glorification and purification of Allah, and end with thanking Him and praising Him. Ibn Kaysān said: They open their speech with monotheism and close it with monotheism.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if God were to hasten for people the evil﴾. Some of them mentioned that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said: ﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal 8:32]. Al-ta'jil (hastening) is bringing a thing forward before its time. Regarding the intended meaning of the verse there are two opinions:

The first: "And if God were to hasten for people the evil" when they invoke curses upon themselves in anger, or upon their families, and they seek its hastening, just as He hastens good for them, they would be destroyed. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

(p-12) The second: "And if God were to hasten for the disbelievers the punishment for their disbelief, just as He hastened for them the worldly good of wealth and children, He would hasten for them the ending of their terms, so that they might hasten the punishment of the Hereafter." This is related by al-Mawardi. What strengthens this view is the completion of the verse and the occasion of its revelation. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "laqudiya ilayhim" with a dammah on the qaf, "ajaluhum" with a dammah on the lam. Ibn 'Amir read "laqada" with a fathah on the qaf, "ajalahum" with a fathah on the lam. We have already mentioned, at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah (2:15), the meaning of al-tughyan (transgression) and al-'amah (blind wandering).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches man﴾ — the scholars differed concerning who it was revealed about, on two views. The first: it was revealed about Abu Hudhayfah, whose name was Hashim ibn al-Mughirah ibn Abdullah al-Makhzumi; this was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. The second: it was revealed about Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; this was said by Ata'. And "al-durr" (harm) means hardship and adversity. The lam in His saying "to his side" (li-janbihi) has the sense of "upon" (ʿala). And concerning the meaning of the verse there are two views: the first: when harm touches him, he calls upon Us lying on his side, or sitting, or standing; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: when harm touches him in these states, he calls upon Us; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But when We remove from him his harm, he passes on﴾ — concerning it there are three views.

The first: he turned away from supplication; this was said by Muqatil. The second: he passed on in well-being as he was before he was tested, and did not take heed from what befell him; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The third: he passed on, tyrannical, neglecting to give thanks.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿as if he had never called upon Us﴾ — al-Zajjaj said: "ka-an" here is the lightened form of the heavy one; the meaning is: "as if he had never called upon Us." Al-Khansa' said:

Ka-an lam yakununa himan yuttaqa, idh al-nasu idh dhaka man ʿazza bazza
(As if they had never been a protected sanctuary to be feared, when people in that time—whoever was mighty, prevailed.)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus has the deeds of the transgressors been made attractive to them﴾ — the meaning: just as supplication in time of trial was made attractive to this disbeliever, and turning away in time of ease, so likewise were the deeds of the transgressors made attractive to them—those who exceed the limit in disbelief and disobedience.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had already destroyed the generations before you﴾. Muqatil said: "This is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah." The word "wrongdoing" (al-zulm) here means shirk (associating partners with God).

Regarding His saying: ﴿and they were not going to believe﴾, there are two views. The first is that it refers to the people of Makkah, as Muqatil said. The second is that it refers to the earlier generations, as Abu Sulayman said. Ibn al-Anbari said: "God imposed upon them the abandonment of faith because of their obstinacy against the truth and their preference for falsehood." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is possible that He made their recompense the sealing of their hearts, and it is possible that He informed them of what was already known about them."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾, meaning: We punish and destroy. "The criminal people" means the polytheists among your people.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We made you successors﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: We made you, O community of Muhammad (ﷺ), successors, meaning: We made you successors in the earth. Qatada said: Allah made us successors only so that He might look at our deeds, so show Allah good deeds from yourselves by night and by day.

(p-14) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾. The scholars differed as to who this was revealed about, on two views. One is that it was revealed about those among the people of Makkah who mocked the Qur'an; this was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it was revealed about the polytheists of Makkah; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah. By "the verses" is meant the Qur'an. "Yarjuna" (who do not expect) is in the sense of "yakhafuna" (who fear). As to the reason for their request for something other than this Qur'an, or for its alteration, there are two views. One is that they wanted the verse of punishment changed into mercy, and the verse of mercy changed into punishment; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that they disliked its mention of resurrection and rising again, since they did not believe in it, and they disliked its disparagement of their gods, so they sought something free of these; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The difference between altering it and bringing something else is that altering it cannot be done while it remains, whereas bringing something other than it may be done while it remains.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for me﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr vowelled this ya' (the final "ya" of "li", i.e., "liya") with a vowel; the rest made it sukun (unvowelled). "Min tilqa'i nafsi" (from my own accord): Nafi' and Abu 'Amr vowelled it; the rest made it sukun. The meaning is: "from my own self," so the meaning is that what I have brought is from Allah, not from myself, so that I would alter it. ﴿Indi akhafu﴾ (Indeed, I fear): Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr opened this ya' (with a fatha). ﴿If I disobey my Lord﴾, that is, in altering it or changing it, ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection.

Section

The scholars of abrogation (naskh) and abrogated (mansukh) have spoken about this verse, as we explained regarding its counterpart in (al-An'am: 15). The purpose of the two verses is to threaten those who oppose; and this was attributed to the Messenger so that the matter would be more severe for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you"﴾. He means the Qur'an. The reason is that He had not sent it down to me so that He would command me to recite it to you. ﴿Nor would He have made it known to you﴾: that is, Allah would not have informed you of it.

Ibn Kathir recited "wa-la-adrakum" with the emphatic lam (lam al-tawkid) and without an alif after it, making it a lam that entered upon "adrakum". Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "udrikum" with imalah (the inclination of the vowel toward i). al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Shaybah ibn Nisah recited "wa-la adra'tukum" with a ta' between the alif and the kaf.

﴿So I have indeed remained among you a lifetime (ʿumuran)﴾. al-Hasan and al-A'mash recited "ʿumran" with the mim sukun. Abu 'Ubayda said: there are three dialects for ʿumr: ʿumr, ʿumur, and ʿamr. Ibn 'Abbas said: I stayed among you forty years without telling you anything of the Qur'an. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ — that it is not from me.

﴿Who is more wicked than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ He means: I did not fabricate against Allah nor did I lie about Him, whereas you did that when you claimed that He has a partner. Here, "al-mujrimun" refers to the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you"﴾. He means the Qur'an. The reason is that He had not sent it down to me so that He would command me to recite it to you. ﴿Nor would He have made it known to you﴾: that is, Allah would not have informed you of it.

Ibn Kathir recited "wa-la-adrakum" with the emphatic lam (lam al-tawkid) and without an alif after it, making it a lam that entered upon "adrakum". Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "udrikum" with imalah (the inclination of the vowel toward i). al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Shaybah ibn Nisah recited "wa-la adra'tukum" with a ta' between the alif and the kaf.

﴿So I have indeed remained among you a lifetime (ʿumuran)﴾. al-Hasan and al-A'mash recited "ʿumran" with the mim sukun. Abu 'Ubayda said: there are three dialects for ʿumr: ʿumr, ʿumur, and ʿamr. Ibn 'Abbas said: I stayed among you forty years without telling you anything of the Qur'an. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ — that it is not from me.

﴿Who is more wicked than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ He means: I did not fabricate against Allah nor did I lie about Him, whereas you did that when you claimed that He has a partner. Here, "al-mujrimun" refers to the polytheists.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say﴾, meaning the polytheists. ﴿These﴾, meaning the idols. Abu 'Ubayda said: their pronoun came in the form of the pronoun used for human beings. We have already discussed this meaning in (al-A'raf: 191), at His saying: "and they are created."

Regarding His saying ﴿our intercessors with Allah﴾, there are two views. The first is that they are our intercessors in the Hereafter. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and by Muqatil. The second is that they are our intercessors in arranging our livelihoods in this world, because they do not affirm the resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on earth?﴾ Al-Dahhak said: Do you inform Allah that He has a partner, when Allah knows of no partner for Himself in the heavens or on earth?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 19:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was but one community, then they differed﴾. This has been explained in surah al-Baqarah (2:213). The best of the opinions is that they were upon one religion, monotheists, then they differed and worshipped idols. The first whom He sent to them was Nuh (peace be upon him).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾. In this there are three opinions.

The first: "Had it not been for a word that preceded," regarding the deferral of this community, that He would not destroy them with punishment as He destroyed those before them, then the matter would have been decided between them by the descent of the punishment, and that would have been a judgment between them concerning what they differed about in religion.

The second: the word is that for every community there is a term, and for the world there is a duration that cannot be advanced beyond its time.

The third: the word is that He does not seize anyone except after the establishment of proof against him.

As for His saying: ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾, there are two opinions: the first is that the matter would have been decided between them by the establishment of the Hour. The second is by the descent of punishment upon the deniers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 20:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say﴾ — meaning the polytheists — ﴿"Why"﴾ (law la), i.e., "Why not" (halla) — ﴿"has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ — like the staff and the hand, and the signs of the prophets. ﴿So say: "The unseen belongs only to Allah."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: your question, "Why has the sign not been sent down?" is a matter of the unseen, and none knows the reason for its withholding except Allah.

The second: when the sign will be sent down is a matter of the unseen, and none knows it except Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So wait﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions: One of them: wait for the sign to be sent down. The second: wait for Allah's judgment between us, by manifesting the one who is in the right over the one who is in the wrong.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We let the people taste mercy﴾. The occasion of its revelation: when the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked drought upon the people of Makkah, and they suffered famine for seven years, Abu Sufyan came to him and said: "Pray for us for abundance; if we are given abundance, we will believe you." So he prayed for them and they were given rain, but they did not believe. This was related by al-Mawardi (al-Mawardi). The exegetes said: what is meant by "the people" here is the disbelievers. Regarding the meaning of "mercy" and "adversity" there are three opinions:

One: that mercy is well-being and joy, and adversity is poverty and affliction; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: mercy is Islam, and adversity is disbelief; this applies to the hypocrites; this was said by al-Hasan.

The third: mercy is abundance, and adversity is drought; this was said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding the meaning of "plotting" (makr) here there are four opinions: One, that it is mockery and denial; this was said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

The second: that it is denial and rejection; this was said by Abu Ubaydah.

The third: that it is attributing blessings to other than Allah, so they say: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (nawʾ)"; this was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The fourth: that makr is hypocrisy, because it is showing faith while concealing disbelief; this was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Allah is swifter in plotting﴾, i.e., in recompense for the plotting. ﴿Indeed, Our messengers﴾, meaning the guardian angels, ﴿record what you plot﴾, i.e., they preserve that record in order to requite you for it. Ya'qub, except Ruways and Abu Hatim, and Aban from Asim, read "yamkurun" with the letter ya.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 22–23:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they sailed with them﴾ returns after addressing them to speaking about them in the third person. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever puts the absent in the place of one being addressed may return to the absent, as the poet said:

؎ "The visiting-places of the lovers have become distant, so your pursuit has become difficult for me, O daughter of Makhram."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with a good wind﴾ means gentle. ﴿And they rejoiced in it﴾ because of its gentleness. ﴿Then there came upon it﴾ meaning the ship. Al-Farra' said: If you wish, you may make it refer to the wind, as if you said: there came upon the good wind a violent wind (ʿāṣif). The Arabs say ʿāṣif and ʿāṣifah, and the wind has blustered (ʿaṣafat) and become violent (aʿṣafat), and the alif is the dialect of the Banu Asad. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-rīḥ al-ʿāṣif is the severe one. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said ʿaṣafat al-rīḥ, so it is ʿāṣif and ʿāṣifah, and aʿṣafat, so it is muʿṣif and muʿṣifah. ﴿And the waves came to them from every place﴾ meaning from every place of the waves.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they thought﴾ has two interpretations: One of them: it means certainty. The second: it means supposition. Regarding His saying "they were encompassed" there are two views:

One of them: they drew near to destruction. Ibn Qutaybah said: The origin of this is that when an enemy surrounds a land, its people have drawn near to destruction. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of anyone who falls into affliction: "So-and-so has been encompassed," meaning the affliction has encompassed him.

The second: the angels encompassed them, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They called upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ apart from their idols. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They abandoned association (shirk) and devoted lordship (rubūbiyyah) to Allah alone, and they said: ﴿If You deliver us from this﴾ violent wind ﴿we will surely be among the thankful﴾, meaning: among the monotheists (muwaḥḥidīn).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They commit injustice on the earth﴾. Al-baghy (transgression): the spreading out into corruption. Al-Asmaʿi said: It is said: "The wound has baghā," when it spreads toward corruption. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They commit injustice on the earth by calling to the worship of other than Allah and by acting in disobedience and corruption.

﴿O mankind﴾ meaning the people of Makkah. ﴿Your injustice is only against yourselves﴾, meaning: the crime of your wrongdoings among you is against yourselves. Al-Zajjaj said: Your deeds of injustice return upon you.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The enjoyment of the worldly life﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Razin, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Hafs, and Aban, from ʿAsim, recited: "matāʿa al-ḥayāti al-dunyā" with the accusative on matāʿ. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads matāʿ in the nominative, the meaning is that what you obtain by this transgression is only what you benefit from in the world; and whoever reads it in the accusative, it is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), so the meaning is: you are given enjoyment, the enjoyment of the worldly life. Abu al-Mutawakkil, al-Yazidi in his selection, and Harun al-ʿAtaki from ʿAsim recited: "matāʿi al-ḥayāh" with a kasrah on the ʿayn. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "matāʿu al-ḥayāti al-dunyā" means: a benefit in the world.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 22–23:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they sailed with them﴾ returns after addressing them to speaking about them in the third person. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever puts the absent in the place of one being addressed may return to the absent, as the poet said:

؎ "The visiting-places of the lovers have become distant, so your pursuit has become difficult for me, O daughter of Makhram."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with a good wind﴾ means gentle. ﴿And they rejoiced in it﴾ because of its gentleness. ﴿Then there came upon it﴾ meaning the ship. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they thought﴾ has two interpretations: One of them: it means certainty. The second: it means supposition. Regarding His saying "they were encompassed" there are two views:

One of them: they drew near to destruction. Ibn Qutaybah said: The origin of this is that when an enemy surrounds a land, its people have drawn near to destruction. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of anyone who falls into affliction: "So-and-so has been encompassed," meaning the affliction has encompassed him.

The second: the angels encompassed them, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They called upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ apart from their idols. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They abandoned association (shirk) and devoted lordship (rubūbiyyah) to Allah alone, and they said: ﴿If You deliver us from this﴾ violent wind ﴿we will surely be among the thankful﴾, meaning: among the monotheists (muwaḥḥidīn).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They commit injustice on the earth﴾. Al-baghy (transgression): the spreading out into corruption. Al-Asmaʿi said: It is said: "The wound has baghā," when it spreads toward corruption. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They commit injustice on the earth by calling to the worship of other than Allah and by acting in disobedience and corruption.

﴿O mankind﴾ meaning the people of Makkah. ﴿Your injustice is only against yourselves﴾, meaning: the crime of your wrongdoings among you is against yourselves. Al-Zajjaj said: Your deeds of injustice return upon you.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The enjoyment of the worldly life﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Razin, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Hafs, and Aban, from ʿAsim, recited: "matāʿa al-ḥayāti al-dunyā" with the accusative on matāʿ. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads matāʿ in the nominative, the meaning is that what you obtain by this transgression is only what you benefit from in the world; and whoever reads it in the accusative, it is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), so the meaning is: you are given enjoyment, the enjoyment of the worldly life. Abu al-Mutawakkil, al-Yazidi in his selection, and Harun al-ʿAtaki from ʿAsim recited: "matāʿi al-ḥayāh" with a kasrah on the ʿayn. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "matāʿu al-ḥayāti al-dunyā" means: a benefit in the world.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 24:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the example of the life of this world is like rain which We send down from the sky﴾. This is a parable that Allah struck for the transient world. He likened it to rain that descends from the sky, ﴿and the plants of the earth mix with it﴾, meaning the vegetation becomes intertwined through the rain and multiplies, ﴿of that which men eat﴾ from grains and other things, ﴿and livestock﴾ from pasture. ﴿Until, when the earth has taken on its adornment﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: its adornment is by vegetation. The origin of zukhruf (adornment) is gold; then it is said of decoration, brightness, flowers, and everything that is embellished: zukhruf. Al-Zajjaj said: zukhruf is the perfection of a thing's beauty.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and it is beautified (wazzayyanat)﴾. The majority recited wazzayyanat with a shaddah (tashdid). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, and Ibn Ya'mar recited it with a fatḥah on the hamzah and with the zay sukun, in the pattern of "wa-af'alat" (wa-azyanat). Al-Zajjaj said: whoever recites "wazzayyanat" with a shaddah, the meaning is "wa-tazayyanat" (and it adorned itself), the taa is assimilated into the zay, the zay is made sukun, and so an alif of connection (alif al-wasl) is brought for it. And whoever recites "wa-azyanat" with the lightened form, on the pattern of af'alat, the meaning is: it came with adornment. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-tazayyanat."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and its people think﴾, i.e., the people of the earth become certain ﴿that they are capable of it﴾, i.e., of what it has produced. He reports about the earth while meaning the vegetation, because the meaning is understood. ﴿Then Our command comes to it﴾, i.e., Our decree to destroy it, ﴿and We make it as harvested stubble﴾, i.e., cut down with nothing left in it. Ḥaṣīd (harvested) means that which is cut and uprooted. ﴿As if it had not flourished yesterday﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it was not inhabited. Al-Maghani are the dwellings which people inhabit by dwelling in them. It is said: "ghanina bil-makan" when they settled in it. Al-Hasan recited "ka'an lam yaghna" with the yā', meaning the harvested stubble. Some exegetes said: (p-22) The interpretation of the verse: the life of this world is a cause for the gathering of wealth and whatever delights and pleases of the world's splendor, until that is complete for its owner, and he thinks he is enjoying it, then it is taken from him by his death or by an event that destroys him, just as water is the cause of the intertwining and abundance of plants. When the earth becomes adorned by it and people think they are enjoying it, Allah destroys it, and what was in it becomes as if it had never been.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 25–26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾ — meaning Paradise. We have already mentioned the meaning of its being named so at His saying: ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 127]. Know that Allah generalizes the call and particularizes guidance to whomever He wills, because the judgment belongs to Him over His creation.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿the Straight Path﴾ there are four sayings:

The first: it is the Book of Allah, narrated by Ali from the Prophet (ﷺ). The second: it is Islam, narrated by al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an from the Prophet (ﷺ). The third: it is the Truth, said by Mujahid and Qatadah. The fourth: it is that which brings out from misguidance and doubts, said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

(p-23) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who did good﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they said, "There is no god but Allah." Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Husna (the good) is a word that needs no description or qualification, because the Arabs use it for the beloved, desired and joyful state. What the Arabs have learned of its usage suffices instead of its description. Likewise, what is added to it is understood by its meaning and recognized through it. This is shown by the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"When we contested the talk and she became yielding, I bent down a branch with clustered tips, swaying,
So we turned to the good (al-husna), our speech grew tender, and I tamed her, and she submitted, a difficult taming, what a humiliation!"

That is: to the desired matter. "Hasartu" means "I pulled." "The branch" is a metaphor for the woman. The "ba'" here emphasizes the speech, as the Arabs say: "He threw his hand to destruction," meaning "he threw his hand." "Al-shamarikh" is a metaphor for the locks. "Rudtu" means "I humbled." For this reason he said "a humiliation" and did not say "a taming."

(p-24) The commentators have five sayings regarding the meaning of al-Husna:

The first: it is Paradise, narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and most of them said so. The second: it is one good deed multiplied by ten, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The third: it is victory, said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit. The fourth: it is the reward in the Hereafter, said by Ibn Zayd. The fifth: it is the hope, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Regarding al-Ziyadah (the increase) there are six sayings:

The first: it is looking at Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Muslim narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Suhayb that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'The increase is looking at the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.'" By this view said Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Huthayfah, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second: that the increase is a chamber of a single pearl having four doors, narrated by al-Hakam from Ali, and it is not authentic.

(p-25) The third: that the increase is the multiplication of a good deed to ten times its like, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The fourth: that the increase is forgiveness and good pleasure, said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that the increase is that what He gave them in this world He will not call them to account for on the Day of Resurrection, said by Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: that the increase is whatever they desire, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there will not cover their faces﴾ — i.e., will not overspread them ﴿dust (qatar)﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-A'mash read "qatr" with a sukun on the ta'. Regarding it there are four sayings:

The first: it is blackness. Ibn 'Abbas said: the blackness of faces from grief. al-Zajjaj said: al-qutar is dust accompanied by blackness. The second: it is the smoke of Hell, said by 'Ata'. The third: it is disgrace, said by Mujahid. The fourth: it is dust, said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

Regarding "dhillah" (humiliation) there are two sayings:

The first: it is grief, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is abasement, said by Abu Sulayman.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 25–26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾ — meaning Paradise. We have already mentioned the meaning of its being named so at His saying: ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 127]. Know that Allah generalizes the call and particularizes guidance to whomever He wills, because the judgment belongs to Him over His creation.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿the Straight Path﴾ there are four sayings:

The first: it is the Book of Allah, narrated by Ali from the Prophet (ﷺ). The second: it is Islam, narrated by al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an from the Prophet (ﷺ). The third: it is the Truth, said by Mujahid and Qatadah. The fourth: it is that which brings out from misguidance and doubts, said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

(p-23) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who did good﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they said, "There is no god but Allah." Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Husna (the good) is a word that needs no description or qualification, because the Arabs use it for the beloved, desired and joyful state. What the Arabs have learned of its usage suffices instead of its description. Likewise, what is added to it is understood by its meaning and recognized through it. This is shown by the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"When we contested the talk and she became yielding, I bent down a branch with clustered tips, swaying,
So we turned to the good (al-husna), our speech grew tender, and I tamed her, and she submitted, a difficult taming, what a humiliation!"

That is: to the desired matter. "Hasartu" means "I pulled." "The branch" is a metaphor for the woman. The "ba'" here emphasizes the speech, as the Arabs say: "He threw his hand to destruction," meaning "he threw his hand." "Al-shamarikh" is a metaphor for the locks. "Rudtu" means "I humbled." For this reason he said "a humiliation" and did not say "a taming."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 27:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they practised shirk (associating partners with God). ﴿The recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent﴾: in the verse there is an omitted element, and concerning its estimated form (taqdir) there are two opinions:

The first: that in it there is an implied "for them" (lahum), the meaning being: for them is the recompense of an evil deed, its equivalent. Tha'lab recited:

"If the slanderers ask about him, then say to them, 'And that is a generous gift for the slanderers.'"

"He has visited Layla briefly, then indeed he is one who departs from Layla after that, and one who prolongs [the separation]."

He meant: "He is one who visits" (muladdim). This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: that in it there is an implied "from them" (minhum), the meaning being: the recompense of an evil deed from them is its equivalent. The Arabs say: "I saw the people, a fasting one and a standing one," meaning: from them is a fasting one and a standing one. Al-Farra' recited:

"Until, when the dawn lit up in the darkness, and the plants were left, some twisted and some mown."

That is, "from it is some twisted," and this is the view of Ibn al-Anbari. Some of them said: the "ba'" (bi-) here is extra (za'idah), and "min" in His saying ﴿from any protector (min 'asim)﴾ is connective (silah), and al-'asim means the one who prevents. ﴿As if their faces had been covered﴾, i.e., were clothed in "qita'an" (pieces). Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read "qita'an" with a fatha on the ta', and it is the plural of qit'ah (piece). Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿qit'an﴾ with the ta' sukun. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the name of that which is cut off. Ibn Jarir said: He said ﴿dark (muzliman)﴾ and did not say "muzlimah" because the meaning is: pieces of the dark night; then the alif and lam of "al-muzlim" were removed, and since it became indefinite while being an attribute of the night, it was put in the accusative as a qat' (distinguishing construction). Some people call what is like this a hal (circumstantial state), and some call it qata'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 28–29:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Day We will gather them all together﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the disbelievers and their gods will be gathered. ﴿Then We will say to those who associated partners [with Allah], "Stay in your place, you and your partners"﴾, that is, your gods. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH; grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: "مكانكم" (makānakum, "your place") is in the accusative as an imperative, as if it were said to them: "Wait in your place until We separate you." The Arabs use it in a threat, saying "makānaka," meaning "wait in your place," so it is a word that has come to be used in the sense of a threat.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We will separate them﴾. Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "فزايلنا" (fazāylanā) with an alif. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "We separated them from one another and from their gods." Ibn Qutaybah said: it is from zāla yazūlu, and azaltuhu (I removed it). Ibn Jarir said: He said "fazayyalnā" and not "fazilnā" in order to indicate the repetition and intensification of the action.

If it is asked: "How can separation occur between them when they are together in the Fire, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]?"

The answer: the separation occurs through the disavowal of every object of worship by those who worshipped it, which is His saying: ﴿And their partners will say﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: their gods. Allah will give speech to the idols, and they will say: ﴿You did not used to worship us﴾, that is, we do not know of your worship of us, because there was no spirit in us. So the worshippers will say: "Yes, indeed we worshipped you," and the gods will say: ﴿Sufficient is Allah as a witness between us and you; indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾, that is, we did not know of it. Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿in kunnā﴾" (in kunnā, "indeed we were") means: "we were only unaware."

If it is asked: what is the reason for the particle "bi" (bi, "with") entering into His saying: ﴿Sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾?

There are two answers concerning this. The first: it entered for emphasis in praise, as they say: "Excellent is ʿAbd Allah," "Noble is ʿAbd al-Rahman," "Enough is our brother," "Sufficient is our friend." This is the view of al-Farra' and his companions. The second: it entered for the emphasis of the speech, since its omission is possible, as one says: "Take hold of the rope" and "Take the rope." This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 30:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Hunalika tabluu﴾ (There, every soul will experience what it did). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "tabluu" with a ba' (ب). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Zayd on the authority of Ya'qub read "tatluu" with a ta' (ت). (p-28) Al-Zajjaj said: "Hunalika" is an adverb of place (zarf), and the meaning is: at that time you will experience. It is in the accusative case governed by "tabluu," except that it is indeclinable (ghayr mutamakkin). The lam is extra (za'idah), and the original form is "hunaka." The lam was given a kasra because of its sukun and the sukun of the alif, and the kaf is for addressing the second person. "Tabluu" means "takhtabiru," i.e., "ta'lamu" (you come to know). As for the one who reads "tatluu" with two ta's, al-Akhfash and others have explained it as "tatluu" from at-tilawah, meaning "taqra'u" (recites). They also explained it as: "every soul follows what it has sent forth." A similar example is the saying of the poet:

Indeed my bucket has made me heavy (tastatlini), and I do not desire to follow the companion.

Meaning: it makes me follow it (tastatbi'uni), i.e., because of its heaviness it calls upon me to follow it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wa-ruddu﴾ (And they will be returned), i.e., in the Hereafter, ﴿ila Allahi mawlahumu al-haqq﴾ (to God, their true Master), who truly holds their affair, not those whom they associated with Him as partners. ﴿Wa-dalla 'anhum﴾ (and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them), i.e., will depart and perish ﴿ma kanu yaftaruna﴾ (of the deities they invented).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Who provides for you from the sky"﴾ [i.e., the rain], "and from the earth" [i.e., the plants], ﴿or who controls hearing﴾ [i.e., the creation of hearing and sight]. The meaning of bringing the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living has already been discussed [in the commentary on Al 'Imran: 27].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who arranges the affair?﴾ [i.e., the affair of this world and the Hereafter.] ﴿They will say, "Allah."﴾ Because they were addressed with what none can do except Allah, and in that is evidence of His oneness (tawhid).

Regarding His saying: ﴿Then will you not fear Him?﴾ there are two views. One is: "Will you not take heed?", said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is: "Will you not fear shirk (associating partners with Allah)?", said by Muqatil.

(p-29) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So that is Allah, your true Lord.﴾ Al-Khattabi said: al-Haqq (the Truth) is that whose existence is established, and everything whose existence and being is sound is ḥaqq.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: How are your minds turned away to the worship of one who provides no sustenance, gives no life, and causes no death?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 33–35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus has the word of your Lord been justified﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ" (kalimatu rabbika, in the singular), and likewise at the end of the surah. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read both instances as "كَلِماتُ" (kalimat, in the plural).

Al-Zajjaj said: The *kaf* in "كَذَلِكَ" (kadhalika, "thus") is in the accusative position, meaning: "Like their deeds, your Lord has recompensed them." The meaning is: it was decreed against them that they would not believe. His saying, ﴿that they do not believe﴾, is a *badal* (substitution, an appositive) for "كَلِمَةِ رَبِّكَ" (the word of your Lord). It is also permissible that the word was justified against them because they do not believe, and that "the word" refers to what they were promised of punishment.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two views concerning "كَذَلِكَ" (thus):

(p-30) One: it refers back to the verbal noun of "تُصْرَفُونَ" (tusrafun, "you are turned away"), so the meaning is: "Just as that turning away occurred, the word of your Lord was justified."

Two: it means "هَكَذا" (hakadha, "in this manner").

Concerning the meaning of "حَقَّتْ" (haqqat, "was justified"), there are two views: one, it became obligatory (wajabat); two, it preceded (sabaqat).

Concerning "كَلِمَتِهِ" (kalimatihi, "His word"), there are two views: one, it means His promise; two, it means His decree. Whoever reads "كَلِماتِ" (kalimat, plural) makes each of the words through which they were threatened a separate "كَلِمَة" (kalima, word). The meaning of the word has already been explained in (al-A'raf: 137 and 158).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "It is Allah who guides to the truth."﴾ That is, to the truth.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is one who does not guide, unless he is guided, more deserving...﴾ Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Warsh on the authority of Nafi' read "يَهَدِّي" (yahaddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *ha'*, and with *tashdid* (doubling) on the *dal*. Al-Zajjaj said: The original form is "يَهْتَدِي" (yahtadi, "is guided"); the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* (idgham, assimilation of consonants), and its vowel was moved onto the *ha'*. Nafi', except Warsh, and Abu 'Amr read "يَهْدِّي" (yahaddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *sukun* (no vowel) on the *ha'*, and *tashdid* on the *dal*, except that Abu 'Amr would give the *ha'* a slight *fatha* sound (ishmam). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "يَهْدِي" (yahdi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *sukun* on the *ha'*, and no *tashdid* on the *dal*. Abu 'Ali said: The meaning is that they cannot guide others unless they themselves are guided. Had the deaf been guided, they would not have been guided; but since they treated them as those who understand, they were given the same treatment as such.

Yahya ibn Adam reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, "يِهِدِّي" (yihiddi), with a *kasra* on the *ya'* and the *ha'* and *tashdid* on the *dal*. Likewise, Aban and Jabalah reported from al-Mufaddal and 'Abd al-Warith. Al-Zajjaj said: They made the *kasra* follow the *kasra*, and this is a weak reading because of the heaviness of a *kasra* on the *ya'*. Hafs reported from 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i from Abu Bakr from him, "يَهِدِّي" (yahiddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *kasra* on the *ha'* and *tashdid* on the *dal*. Al-Zajjaj said: This is, in its soundness, like the reading with a *fatha* on the *ha'*, except that the *ha'* was given a *kasra* because two unvocalized consonants met. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "يَهْتَدِي" (yahtadi) with an added *ta'*.

By His saying "أمْ مَن لا يَهِدِّي" (am man la yahiddi, "or one who does not guide"), the intended referent is the deaf, ﴿unless he is guided﴾. The apparent sense of the speech indicates that the idols, if they were guided, would be guided; but this is not the case, since they are stones that cannot be guided. However, because they had taken them as gods, He spoke of them as one speaks of those who understand, and they were described with the attributes of those who understand, even though in reality they are not so. For this reason He said in describing them "أمَّنْ" (amman, "or one who"), since they treated them as those who understand. And when He gave them their due in their original status, He said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ (Maryam: 42).

Al-Farra' said: "أمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي" means: "Do you worship that which cannot move from its place unless it is moved?" Some have directed the speech toward the leaders and the misleaders, but the first view is more sound.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: This is a complete sentence, as if it were said to them: "What is the matter with you in worshipping idols?" Then it was said to them: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ That is: "In what condition do you judge?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "How do you decide for yourselves?" Muqatil said: "How do you decide with injustice?"

Likewise, Aban and Jabalah reported from al-Mufaddal and 'Abd al-Warith. Al-Zajjaj said: They made the *kasra* follow the *kasra*, and this is a weak reading because of the heaviness of a *kasra* on the *ya'*. Hafs reported from 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i from Abu Bakr from him, "يَهِدِّي" (yahiddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *kasra* on the *ha'* and *tashdid* on the *dal*. Al-Zajjaj said: This is, in its soundness, like the reading with a *fatha* on the *ha'*, except that the *ha'* was given a *kasra* because two unvocalized consonants met. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "يَهْتَدِي" (yahtadi) with an added *ta'*.

By His saying "أمْ مَن لا يَهِدِّي" (am man la yahiddi, "or one who does not guide"), the intended referent is the deaf, ﴿unless he is guided﴾. The apparent sense of the speech indicates that the idols, if they were guided, would be guided; but this is not the case, since they are stones that cannot be guided. However, because they had taken them as gods, He spoke of them as one speaks of those who understand, and they were described with the attributes of those who understand, even though in reality they are not so. For this reason He said in describing them "أمَّنْ" (amman, "or one who"), since they treated them as those who understand. And when He gave them their due in their original status, He said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ (Maryam: 42).

Al-Farra' said: "أمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي" means: "Do you worship that which cannot move from its place unless it is moved?" Some have directed the speech toward the leaders and the misleaders, but the first view is more sound.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: This is a complete sentence, as if it were said to them: "What is the matter with you in worshipping idols?" Then it was said to them: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ That is: "In what condition do you judge?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "How do you decide for yourselves?" Muqatil said: "How do you decide with injustice?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 33–35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus has the word of your Lord been justified﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ" (kalimatu rabbika, in the singular), and likewise at the end of the surah. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read both instances as "كَلِماتُ" (kalimat, in the plural).

Al-Zajjaj said: The *kaf* in "كَذَلِكَ" (kadhalika, "thus") is in the accusative position, meaning: "Like their deeds, your Lord has recompensed them." The meaning is: it was decreed against them that they would not believe. His saying, ﴿that they do not believe﴾, is a *badal* (substitution, an appositive) for "كَلِمَةِ رَبِّكَ" (the word of your Lord). It is also permissible that the word was justified against them because they do not believe, and that "the word" refers to what they were promised of punishment.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two views concerning "كَذَلِكَ" (thus):

(p-30) One: it refers back to the verbal noun of "تُصْرَفُونَ" (tusrafun, "you are turned away"), so the meaning is: "Just as that turning away occurred, the word of your Lord was justified."

Two: it means "هَكَذا" (hakadha, "in this manner").

Concerning the meaning of "حَقَّتْ" (haqqat, "was justified"), there are two views: one, it became obligatory (wajabat); two, it preceded (sabaqat).

Concerning "كَلِمَتِهِ" (kalimatihi, "His word"), there are two views: one, it means His promise; two, it means His decree. Whoever reads "كَلِماتِ" (kalimat, plural) makes each of the words through which they were threatened a separate "كَلِمَة" (kalima, word). The meaning of the word has already been explained in (al-A'raf: 137 and 158).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "It is Allah who guides to the truth."﴾ That is, to the truth.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is one who does not guide, unless he is guided, more deserving...﴾ Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Warsh on the authority of Nafi' read "يَهَدِّي" (yahaddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *ha'*, and with *tashdid* (doubling) on the *dal*. Al-Zajjaj said: The original form is "يَهْتَدِي" (yahtadi, "is guided"); the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* (idgham, assimilation of consonants), and its vowel was moved onto the *ha'*. Nafi', except Warsh, and Abu 'Amr read "يَهْدِّي" (yahaddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *sukun* (no vowel) on the *ha'*, and *tashdid* on the *dal*, except that Abu 'Amr would give the *ha'* a slight *fatha* sound (ishmam). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "يَهْدِي" (yahdi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *sukun* on the *ha'*, and no *tashdid* on the *dal*. Abu 'Ali said: The meaning is that they cannot guide others unless they themselves are guided. Had the deaf been guided, they would not have been guided; but since they treated them as those who understand, they were given the same treatment as such.

Yahya ibn Adam reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, "يِهِدِّي" (yihiddi), with a *kasra* on the *ya'* and the *ha'* and *tashdid* on the *dal*. Likewise, Aban and Jabalah reported from al-Mufaddal and 'Abd al-Warith. Al-Zajjaj said: They made the *kasra* follow the *kasra*, and this is a weak reading because of the heaviness of a *kasra* on the *ya'*. Hafs reported from 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i from Abu Bakr from him, "يَهِدِّي" (yahiddi), with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *kasra* on the *ha'* and *tashdid* on the *dal*. Al-Zajjaj said: This is, in its soundness, like the reading with a *fatha* on the *ha'*, except that the *ha'* was given a *kasra* because two unvocalized consonants met. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "يَهْتَدِي" (yahtadi) with an added *ta'*.

By His saying "أمْ مَن لا يَهِدِّي" (am man la yahiddi, "or one who does not guide"), the intended referent is the deaf, ﴿unless he is guided﴾. The apparent sense of the speech indicates that the idols, if they were guided, would be guided; but this is not the case, since they are stones that cannot be guided. However, because they had taken them as gods, He spoke of them as one speaks of those who understand, and they were described with the attributes of those who understand, even though in reality they are not so. For this reason He said in describing them "أمَّنْ" (amman, "or one who"), since they treated them as those who understand. And when He gave them their due in their original status, He said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?﴾ (Maryam: 42).

Al-Farra' said: "أمَّنْ لا يَهِدِّي" means: "Do you worship that which cannot move from its place unless it is moved?" Some have directed the speech toward the leaders and the misleaders, but the first view is more sound.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: This is a complete sentence, as if it were said to them: "What is the matter with you in worshipping idols?" Then it was said to them: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ That is: "In what condition do you judge?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "How do you decide for yourselves?" Muqatil said: "How do you decide with injustice?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 36:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And most of them follow not except assumption﴾, that is, all of them. ﴿Except assumption﴾, that is, they do not know with certainty that they are gods, but rather they assume something and then follow it. ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾, that is, it is not like certainty, and it does not take the place of the truth. Muqatil said: their assumption that they are gods does not avert from them any of the punishment. Others said: their assumption that they will intercede for them does not avail them.

(p-32) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not [possible] for this Qur'an that it be fabricated (yuftara) apart from Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: This is the answer to their saying: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yunus 10:15], and the answer to their saying: ﴿He has fabricated it﴾ [al-Furqan 25:4].

Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is: it is not fitting for the like of this Qur'an that it be fabricated apart from Allah, so "an" (that) came in the sense of "yanbaghi" (it is fitting). Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible for "an" together with "yuftara" to be a verbal noun (masdar), and its implied construction is: "And this Qur'an was not a fabrication." It is also permissible for "kana" (was) to be complete (taamma), so the meaning becomes: this Qur'an was not sent down, and this Qur'an did not appear, to be fabricated, or by way of being fabricated. Thus "an" is in the accusative by the removal of the governing preposition according to al-Farra', and in the genitive by the implied preposition according to al-Kisa'i. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of "an yuftara" is: it is attributed to other than Allah, or it is invented.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But [it is] a confirmation of what was before it﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

The first: that it is the confirmation of the earlier Scriptures (al-kutub al-mutaqaddima). This was said by Ibn Abbas. According to this, He said "alladhi" (that which) because He means the revelation (al-wahy).

The second: what is before it of the resurrection and the rising (al-ba'th wa al-nushur). This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: the confirmation of the Prophet ﷺ who was before the Qur'an, because they witnessed the Prophet ﷺ and knew him before they heard the Qur'an. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a detailing of the Book﴾, that is: and the clarification of the Book which Allah prescribed for the community of Muhammad ﷺ, the obligations (al-fara'id) which He imposed upon them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 38:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Regarding "ʾam" (or) there are two opinions. The first: it means "wa" (and), said by Abu ʿUbayda. The second: it means "bal" (rather), said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-33) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Bring a surah like a surah from it." He mentioned "like" (mithl) because they were only seeking a resemblance of kind. ﴿And call upon whomever you can besides Allah﴾ from among those who are in denial, like you ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that he fabricated it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of it﴾. There are two views concerning this. The first: the meaning is, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of what it contains of the mention of Paradise and Hellfire, the Resurrection and the recompense. The second: they did not encompass in knowledge the denial of it, because they were in doubt concerning it.

And concerning His saying: ﴿and its interpretation has not yet come to them﴾ there are two views. The first: the fulfilment of what they were promised of threat. Ta'wil (interpretation, here understood as the outcome to which a matter returns) is what the matter returns to. The second: they did not have knowledge of its ta'wil; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

It was said to Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna: People say, "Every person is an enemy of what he is ignorant of." He said: This is in the Book of Allah. It was asked: Where? He said: ﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of it﴾.

It was said to al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl: Do you find in the Qur'an, "Whoever is ignorant of something opposes it"? He said: Yes, in two places. His saying: ﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of it﴾, and His saying: ﴿And since they were not guided by it, they will say, "This is an ancient falsehood"﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:11].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 40:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾. Regarding those referred to, there are two opinions:

(p-34) The first: they are the Jews. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the Quraysh. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

Regarding the pronoun in "bihi" ("in it"), there are two opinions. The first: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his religion. This was said by Muqatil. The second: it refers to the Qur'an. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

This verse includes a report of what has preceded in the knowledge of Allah, so the meaning is: "And among them are those who will believe in it." Al-Zajjaj said: "Among them are those who know that it is the truth and so affirm it, and those who are obstinate and so disbelief becomes apparent. ﴿And among them are those who do not believe in it﴾, meaning: they doubt and do not affirm."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters﴾. 'Ata' said: "He means the deniers," and this is a threat to them.

The Word of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, say: "To me is my deed, and to you is your deed..."﴾ [the verse]. Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas: it was abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf); but this is not correct, because there is no contradiction between the two verses.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. They differed concerning whom it was revealed, in three opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah. They used to come to the Messenger of Allah and listen to the Qur'an; they would be impressed by it and desire it, but wretchedness would prevail over them, so this verse was revealed.

The second: it was revealed concerning the mockers. They used to listen to the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to mock and deny, and they gained nothing from it, so this verse was revealed concerning them. Both opinions are narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh; this was said by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: Their outward state is the outward state of one who listens, but because of the intensity of their enmity they are in the position of the deaf. ﴿And even if they do not understand﴾, i.e., even if they were, along with that, ignorant. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means that they are worse than the deaf, because the deaf have minds and hearts, whereas these ones, Allah has made their hearts deaf.

The Words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means, "astonished at you."

﴿Then can you guide the blind﴾. He means: Allah has blinded their hearts, so they do not see.

Al-Zajjaj said: "And among them are those who turn their gaze toward you, and this is from their hatred of you and their aversion to what they see of your signs, like the blind man."

Ibn Jarir said: "And among them are those who listen to your speech and look at your proofs for your prophethood, but Allah has deprived him of success (tawfiq)."

Muqatil said: "Law" (لَوْ) in the two verses has the meaning of "idha" (إذا, "when").

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all.﴾ When He mentioned those upon whom the decree of wretchedness had preceded, He informed that the ordaining of that upon them is not an injustice, because He disposes of His dominion as He wills. And when they earn sins, they have wronged themselves by that, because the act is attributed to them, even though it is by the decree of Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But the people﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿But the people﴾ with the nun lightened (takhfif) and with kasra, and with the noun after it in the nominative (raf').

(p-36) His saying, Exalted is He: "And the Day We gather them" (wa-yawma nahshuruhum). Hamzah recited it as "yahshuruhum" with the letter ya'. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: they are the polytheists.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As if they had not remained but an hour of the day﴾. In this there are two opinions:

One of them: "As if they had not remained in their graves," reported by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "In the world," reported by Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: "It made the period between their death and their resurrection seem to them the length of an hour of the day, because of the terror of what they faced of the Resurrection."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will recognize one another﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: when they are raised from the graves they recognize one another, then the recognition ends. Al-Zajjaj said: in their recognition of one another, and their knowledge of one another's misguidance of each other, there is rebuke for them and the establishment of proof against them. It was also said: when they recognize one another, some of them rebuke others, so one says to another: "You misled me, and you caused me to enter the Fire."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost﴾. This is from the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, not from their saying. The meaning: they lost the reward of Paradise when they denied the resurrection, ﴿and they were not guided﴾ out of error.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 46–47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾. The exegetes said: The battle of Badr was among what Allah showed him (ﷺ) of their punishment during his lifetime. ﴿Or We cause you to die﴾ before We show you it, ﴿then to Us is their return﴾ after death. The meaning is: if We do not take vengeance upon them quickly, We will take vengeance later.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah is Witness over what they do﴾, of disbelief and denial. Al-Farra' said: "Thumma" (then) here is a conjunction; had it been said that its meaning there is "Allah is Witness," it would have been permissible. Others said: "Thumma" here means "wa" (and). Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "Tha·amma Allahu shahid" with a fatha on the tha', meaning: "There (hunalika) Allah is Witness."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when their messenger comes, judgment is passed between them﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: when he comes in this world, after permission has been given to him to call them, judgment is passed between them by hastening vengeance upon them; this is the view of al-Hasan. Others said: when he comes to them in this world, they are judged, by their following him or opposing him, with obedience and disobedience.

The second: when the Day of Resurrection comes; this is the view of Mujahid. Others said: when he comes as a witness over them.

The third: when he comes on the Resurrection, after they had denied him in this world; this is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Judgment is passed between them with justice﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: the first: between the community, so the doer of good is rewarded and the doer of evil is punished. The second: between them and their Prophet.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 46–47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾. The exegetes said: The battle of Badr was among what Allah showed him (ﷺ) of their punishment during his lifetime. ﴿Or We cause you to die﴾ before We show you it, ﴿then to Us is their return﴾ after death. The meaning is: if We do not take vengeance upon them quickly, We will take vengeance later.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah is Witness over what they do﴾, of disbelief and denial. Al-Farra' said: "Thumma" (then) here is a conjunction; had it been said that its meaning there is "Allah is Witness," it would have been permissible. Others said: "Thumma" here means "wa" (and). Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "Tha·amma Allahu shahid" with a fatha on the tha', meaning: "There (hunalika) Allah is Witness."
