The first: when he comes in this world, after permission has been given to him to call them, judgment is passed between them by hastening vengeance upon them; this is the view of al-Hasan. Others said: when he comes to them in this world, they are judged, by their following him or opposing him, with obedience and disobedience.

The second: when the Day of Resurrection comes; this is the view of Mujahid. Others said: when he comes as a witness over them.

The third: when he comes on the Resurrection, after they had denied him in this world; this is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Judgment is passed between them with justice﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: the first: between the community, so the doer of good is rewarded and the doer of evil is punished. The second: between them and their Prophet.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 48:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ Concerning those who say this, there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the earlier nations, whom He informs about their hastening the punishment against their prophets. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are the polytheists to whom our Prophet ﷺ gave warning. This is the view of Abu Sulayman.

Regarding what is meant by "the promise," there are two opinions. One of them: it is the punishment. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is the establishment of the Hour. ﴿If you are truthful﴾, you and your followers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 49–52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I have no power to bring harm or benefit upon myself...﴾ [the verse], I have already mentioned its tafsir (interpretation) in two verses of (Al-A'raf: 34 and 188).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-bayat (the night attack) is anything that happens at night.

His saying: "madha" (ماذا) is in the nominative position in two respects. The first is that "dha" (ذا) means "alladhi" (the one which), so the meaning is: What is it that the criminals seek to hasten? It is also permissible for "madha" to be a single word, so the meaning is: What thing do the criminals seek to hasten? The pronoun in "minhu" (منه) refers to the punishment. It is also permissible for it to refer to the mention of God, may He be exalted, so the meaning would be: What thing do the criminals seek to hasten from God, may He be exalted? Its reference to the punishment is the better reading, because of His saying: ﴿Only when it has fallen will you then believe in it?﴾.

Some of the mufassirin (commentators) mentioned that the intended "criminals" are the polytheists, who used to say: "We deny the punishment and seek to hasten it, then when the punishment falls, we will believe in it." So God, may He be exalted, rebuked them, saying: ﴿Only when it has fallen will you then believe in it?﴾, meaning: at that time you will believe, but faith will not be accepted from you, and it will be said to you: "Now you believe?" Thus the words "you believe in it" are understood, along with "Now? And you used to seek to hasten it mockingly," which is His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved, at the descent of the punishment, ﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾, because when the punishment descends upon them, they will be led from it to the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I have no power to bring harm or benefit upon myself...﴾ [the verse], I have already mentioned its tafsir (interpretation) in two verses of (Al-A'raf: 34 and 188).

The first is that "dha" (ذا) means "alladhi" (the one which), so the meaning is: What is it that the criminals seek to hasten? It is also permissible for it to refer to the mention of God, may He be exalted, so the meaning would be: What thing do the criminals seek to hasten from God, may He be exalted? Its reference to the punishment is the better reading, because of His saying: ﴿Only when it has fallen will you then believe in it?﴾.

Some of the mufassirin (commentators) mentioned that the intended "criminals" are the polytheists, who used to say: "We deny the punishment and seek to hasten it, then when the punishment falls, we will believe in it." So God, may He be exalted, rebuked them, saying: ﴿Only when it has fallen will you then believe in it?﴾, meaning: at that time you will believe, but faith will not be accepted from you, and it will be said to you: "Now you believe?" Thus the words "you believe in it" are understood, along with "Now? And you used to seek to hasten it mockingly," which is His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved, at the descent of the punishment, ﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾, because when the punishment descends upon them, they will be led from it to the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 49–52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I have no power to bring harm or benefit upon myself...﴾ [the verse], I have already mentioned its tafsir (interpretation) in two verses of (Al-A'raf: 34 and 188).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-bayat (the night attack) is anything that happens at night.

His saying: "madha" (ماذا) is in the nominative position in two respects. The first is that "dha" (ذا) means "alladhi" (the one which), so the meaning is: What is it that the criminals seek to hasten? It is also permissible for "madha" to be a single word, so the meaning is: What thing do the criminals seek to hasten? The pronoun in "minhu" (منه) refers to the punishment. It is also permissible for it to refer to the mention of God, may He be exalted, so the meaning would be: What thing do the criminals seek to hasten from God, may He be exalted? Thus the words "you believe in it" are understood, along with "Now? And you used to seek to hasten it mockingly," which is His saying: ﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved, at the descent of the punishment, ﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾, because when the punishment descends upon them, they will be led from it to the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 53:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?"﴾ That is, they ask you for information, "Is it true?" meaning the Resurrection (al-ba'th) and the punishment (al-'adhab). ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord"﴾ The meaning of "iy" is "na'am" (yes). Nafi' and Abu 'Amr pronounced the yā' of "rabbī" with a fatha. He swore an oath together with his announcement only for emphasis (ta'kid). Ibn Qutaybah said: "iy" has the meaning of "bal" (rather), and it does not come except before an oath, as a connecting particle (sila) for it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you cannot escape it﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "You cannot outrun Him" (bi-sabiqin). Al-Zajjaj said: "You are not among those who can make Him unable to requite them for their disbelief."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verses 54–56:

Allah's words: ﴿And if every soul that had done wrong possessed whatever is on the earth, it would surely offer it as ransom﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "[It means] they associated partners with Allah." ﴿Whatever is on the earth, it would surely offer it as ransom﴾ at the descent of the punishment. ﴿And they will conceal the regret﴾: that is, the leaders concealed it from the followers. ﴿And judgment will be passed between them﴾: that is, between the two groups.

Others, among them Abu 'Ubayda and al-Mufaddal, said: "Asarru al-nadama" (they concealed the regret) means "they showed it," because it is not a day of pretence or patience. Al-Israr (concealment) is among the words with opposite meanings (al-addad). It is said: "asartu al-shay'," meaning "I hid the thing," and "asartuhu," meaning "I revealed it." Al-Farazdaq said:

"When al-Hajjaj saw his sword drawn, the Harurī who had been hiding it revealed it."

That is, he showed it. According to this view, they showed the regret when the Fire was kindled for them, because the Fire distracted them from pretence and concealment. According to the first view, they hid it before the Fire was kindled for them.

Allah's words: ﴿Surely the promise of Allah is true﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: [it refers to] what He promised His friends of reward and what He promised His enemies of punishment. ﴿But most of them﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿do not know﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "[It means] they associated partners with Allah." ﴿Whatever is on the earth, it would surely offer it as ransom﴾ at the descent of the punishment. ﴿And they will conceal the regret﴾: that is, the leaders concealed it from the followers. ﴿And judgment will be passed between them﴾: that is, between the two groups.

Allah's saying: ﴿O mankind﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means Quraysh. ﴿There has certainly come to you an admonition﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿And healing for what is in the breasts﴾, meaning a cure for the disease of ignorance. ﴿And guidance﴾, meaning a clarification away from misguidance.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy﴾, concerning which there are eight opinions:

The first: the bounty of Allah is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah and Hilal ibn Yasaf also said so. It is also reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid in some narrations from them, and it is the choice of Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made them among the people of the Qur'an. This was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said so, as did al-Hasan in one narration.

The third: the bounty of Allah is knowledge, and His mercy is Muhammad (ﷺ). This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: the bounty of Allah is Islam, and His mercy is its adornment in the hearts. This was said by Ibn 'Umar.

The fifth: the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is Islam. This was said by al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam, his son, and Muqatil.

The sixth: the bounty of Allah and His mercy are both the Qur'an. This was related by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

The seventh: the bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is the Sunnah. This was said by Khalid ibn Ma'dan.

The eighth: the bounty of Allah is divine success (tawfiq), and His mercy is protection (ismah). This was said by Ibn 'Uyaynah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So let them rejoice﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Mijlaz, Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it as "fa-lateftarahu" with a ta' (فَلْتَفْرَحُوا). al-Hasan, Mu'adh al-Qari', and Abu al-Mutawakkil read the same way, except that they kasrah the lam (لام). Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran read "fa-bidhalika fafrahu" (فَبِذَلِكَ فافْرَحُوا). Ibn 'Abbas said: "by that bounty and mercy." ﴿It is better than what they accumulate﴾, i.e., than what the disbelievers gather of wealth. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, and Ruways read "tajma'una" with a ta' (تَجْمَعُونَ). Ibn al-Anbari related that the ba' in His saying ﴿in the bounty of Allah﴾ is the predicate of a hidden subject, whose interpretation is: "This is the healing and this is the admonition, by the bounty of Allah and His mercy; so by that favor from Allah, let them rejoice."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: This is an address to the disbelievers of Quraysh, who used to forbid what they wished and permit what they wished. And "sent down" (anzala) here means "created" (khalaqa). We have explained some of their views regarding what they did concerning the bahirah (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was released, forbidden to be ridden or milked) and the sa'ibah (a camel released freely to graze, a term for animals left unburdened for their gods), and other matters, in Surah al-Ma'idah (5:103) and Surah al-An'am (6:139).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you [to do so]?﴾ That is: in this permitting and forbidding.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 60:

(p-42) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what will those who fabricate lies against Allah think [of their fate]?﴾ There is an omitted element in the speech; its implied meaning is: what do they think Allah will do to them on the Day of Resurrection for their lying? ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ in that He did not hasten the punishment upon them, ﴿but most of them do not give thanks﴾ for the delay of the punishment from them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 61:

The Almighty said: ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter﴾ meaning: in any task of the affairs (a'mal). Its plural is shu'un (affairs). ﴿And you do not recite from it﴾ Regarding the pronoun (ha' al-kinaya) in "from it," there are two opinions:

The first: it refers to the matter (al-sha'n). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: at whatever time you are engaged in some matter of the worship of Allah, and whatever you recite of the matter, of the Qur'an.

The second: it refers to Allah, the Exalted, so the meaning is: and what you recite from Allah, that is, of what is revealed from Him of the Qur'an. This was mentioned by a group of scholars. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and his community (ummah) is included in it, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And you do not do any deed﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: He combined them in this to show that they are included in the first two actions.

The Almighty said: ﴿when you are immersed in it﴾ The pronoun (ha') refers to the deed. Ibn Qutayba said: tufidun (you are immersed) means ta'khudhun fihi (you take up with it). Al-Zajjaj said: tantashirun fihi (you spread out in it); it is said: "afada al-qawm fi al-hadith" (the people plunged into the talk) when they spread out in it and got deeply involved. ﴿And there is not hidden﴾ its meaning: and there is not far off. Ibn Qutayba said: (p-43) meaning it is not distant and not absent. Al-Kisa'i read "ya'zib" (with a kasra on the zay) here and in (Saba' 3). We have already explained ﴿an atom's weight﴾ in Surat al-Nisa' (4:40).

The Almighty said: ﴿nor [what is] smaller than that or greater﴾ The majority read the ra' in both words with a fatha. Hamza, Khalaf, and Ya'qub read them with a damma on the ra'. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads with a fatha, the meaning is: and nothing is hidden from your Lord of an atom's weight, nor a weight smaller than that or greater, and the position is one of khafd (genitive), but it is marked with a fatha because it is indeclinable (la yanṣarif). Whoever reads with a damma, the meaning is: nothing is hidden from your Lord, an atom's weight, nor anything smaller or greater. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), so the meaning would be: nor [is there anything] smaller than that or greater. ﴿Except that it is in a clear Book﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 62–64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the friends of Allah—﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas narrated that "a man said: O Messenger of Allah, who are the friends of Allah? He said: 'Those who, when they are seen, Allah is remembered.'" ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Surely among the servants of Allah are people who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets and the martyrs will envy on the Day of Resurrection because of their station with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they, and what are their deeds, that we may love them?" He said: "They are a people who love one another by the Spirit of Allah, without ties of kinship between them and without wealth which they exchange. By Allah, their faces are light, and they are upon pulpits of light. They do not fear when people fear." Then he recited: "Surely the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world.﴾ Concerning it there are three opinions:

One of them: that it is the good dream which a righteous man sees, or which is seen for him. This was narrated by ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, Abu al-Darda, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, and Abu Hurairah from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: that it is the good tidings of the angels to them at the time of death. This was said by al-Dahhak, Qatadah, and al-Zuhri.

The third: that it is what Allah has announced of His Paradise and His reward in His Book, as in His saying: ﴿And give good news to those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25], ﴿and rejoice in the Garden﴾ [Fussilat: 30], ﴿their Lord gives them good news﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21]. This is the view of al-Hasan, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj chose it, and both cited His saying: ﴿There is no alteration in the words of Allah﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There is no breaking of His promises, for His promises are by His words; so if the words are not altered, the promises are not altered."

As for their good news in the Hereafter, there are three opinions:

One of them: that it is the Garden. This was narrated by Abu Hurairah from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Qutaybah chose it.

The second: that at the departure of the soul they are given the good news of the good pleasure of Allah (Ridwan). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that it is at their rising from their graves. This was said by Muqatil.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 65:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Their denial." Others said: "Their unity against you in enmity, their denial, and their harm." The sentence is complete here. Then he began anew and said: ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to Allah﴾, meaning: the victory belongs to Him, so He is your helper and the helper of your religion. ﴿He is the Hearing﴾ of their speech, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of what they conceal, and He will recompense them for that.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 66:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Verily, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Ala" (alā) is an opening of speech and a call to attention, meaning: the One to whom they belong does with them and to them whatever He wills.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners⁠—﴾ That is: they do not really follow partners, because they consider them to be partners of Allah and intercessors for them, but they are not as they suppose. (p. 46) ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾ concerning that, ﴿and they do nothing but guess.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: they lie. Ibn Qutayba said: they conjecture and estimate.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He it is who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾. The meaning: Indeed your Lord, whose lordship you must believe in, is the One who made for you the night that you may rest therein, so that the fatigue and weariness of the day are removed by resting at night. And He made the day ﴿to see by﴾, i.e., bright, so that you may see by it. He attributed the seeing to the day because the listener has understood the intended meaning, since the day does not see; rather it is a time in which others act. This is like His words: ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning a pleasing (marḍiyyah) life. This is like what is said: "a sleeping night" (laylun nā'im). Jarir said:

؎ You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, during the night journey, and you slept, while the night of the mounts is not sleeping.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾, hearing with contemplation (samā' i'tibār), so they know that none is able to do that except the capable God.

(p-47) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means the people of Makkah, who made the angels the daughters of Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him!﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence above what they say. ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ — free of need for a wife or a son. ﴿You have no authority for this.﴾ That is: you have no proof (ḥujjah) for what you say. [Note: "You have no authority for this" renders ﴿إن عندكم من سلطان﴾, i.e., "you have no sultan (authority/proof) for it."]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not prosper.﴾ On this there are three opinions: First, they will not remain in this world. Second, they will not be happy in the final outcome. Third, they will not attain success. Al-Zajjaj said: This is a complete pause (waqf al-tamām), and His saying "an enjoyment in this world" (matāʿun fī al-dunyā) is in the nominative case, meaning: that is an enjoyment in this world.

(p-47) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means the people of Makkah, who made the angels the daughters of Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him!﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence above what they say. ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ — free of need for a wife or a son. ﴿You have no authority for this.﴾ That is: you have no proof (ḥujjah) for what you say. [Note: "You have no authority for this" renders ﴿إن عندكم من سلطان﴾, i.e., "you have no sultan (authority/proof) for it."]

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 71:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And recite to them the news of Noah﴾. In this there is evidence of his prophethood, since he reported the stories of the prophets while he could not read the books; and it is an exhortation to patience, and an admonition to his people by mentioning the people of Noah and the punishment that befell them for their denial.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If my standing [among you] has been grievous﴾, i.e., it has been great and burdensome, ﴿my standing﴾, i.e., the length of my stay. Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Jawza' read "maqami" with a dammah on the mim (muqami). ﴿And my reminding﴾, i.e., my admonition. ﴿Then upon Allah I have relied﴾, in my being helped and in warding off your evil from me. ﴿So determine your plan﴾. The majority read "fa-ajmi'u" with a hamzah and a kasrah on the mim, from "ajma'tu" (I determined). Al-Asma'i related from Nafi': "fajma'u" with a fathah on the mim, from "jama'tu" (I gathered). The meaning of "ajmi'u amrakum" is: make your affair firm and resolve upon it. Al-Mu'arrij said: "ajma'tu al-amr" is more eloquent than "ajma'tu 'alayhi," and he recited:

Oh, would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit: will I ever go forth one day, while my affair is resolved?

As for the narration of al-Asma'i, Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that its meaning is: gather those of authority among you, i.e., your leaders. It is also possible that he made the "affair" to be what they were gathering of their scheming by which they plot, so it is like His saying: ﴿So gather your scheme, then come in line﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your partners﴾. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: and call upon your partners. Al-Zajjaj said: the "waw" here carries the meaning of "ma'a" (with), so the meaning is: with your partners. You say: if the she-camel were left with her young, she would suckle it, i.e., with her young. Ya'qub read "wa-shurakā'ukum" with a raf' (nominative).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then let not your plan be concealed from you﴾. In this there are two opinions: first, let not your affair be hidden, related by Ibn 'Abbas. Second, a grief upon you, as you say "karb" and "kurbah" (distress), related by Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Zajjaj mentioned both opinions. And regarding His saying: ﴿Then carry it out against me﴾ there are two opinions: first, carry out against me what is in your souls, related by Mujahid. Second, do what you intend, related by al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: carry out against me your harm and what you threaten me with, as the Arabs say: "qad qada fulan" (so-and-so has decided), meaning: he died and passed away.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 72–73:

Allah's statement: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, i.e., you turn away from faith. "Then I have not asked you for any wage," i.e., my calling you was not out of greed for your wealth.

(p-49) Allah's statement: ﴿My wage is only﴾. Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ, and Hafs on the authority of ʿAsim vocalized this ya' (with a vowel), while the rest read it with sukun (silent).

Allah's statement: ﴿And We made them successors﴾, i.e., We made those who were saved with Nuh successors (khalaif, plural of khalifah, "successor," "one who comes after") in place of those who perished.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 10, verse 74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent after him messengers to their peoples﴾ — i.e., after Noah — ﴿messengers to their peoples﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means Abraham, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shuʿayb. ﴿And they brought them clear proofs﴾ — i.e., it became clear to them that they were messengers of Allah. ﴿But they were not ones to believe in what they had denied﴾ — i.e., those peoples; it refers to those who came before them. The meaning is that the later ones proceeded upon the same path as the earlier ones in denial. Muqatil said: ﴿They were not ones to believe in what they had denied﴾ of the punishment before its descent.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We seal﴾ — i.e., just as We sealed the hearts of those peoples, ﴿thus do We seal upon the hearts of the transgressors﴾ — meaning those who exceed what they were commanded.

Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verse 75:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then We sent after them﴾ means: the messengers who were sent after Noah.

"When the truth came to them from Us, they said, 'This is clearly magic.'" Verse 76 refers to what Moses brought of the signs.

Allah says: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ Al-Zajjaj (a noted grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: The meaning is: Do you say of the truth, when it has come to you, this statement, which is their saying: ﴿Indeed, this is clear magic﴾? Then he confronted them, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ Ibn al-Anbari (a grammarian and exegete) said: They introduced the alif only to express the gravity of the matter, as a man says when he sees a fine garment: "Is this a garment?", meaning by the question to magnify it. And a man who receives a gift says: "Is what I see true?", magnifying what has reached him. Others said: The sense of the sentence is: Do you say of the truth when it has come to you that it is magic, "Is this magic?" So the first word "magic" is omitted, being understood from the context, as in His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, they will distress your faces﴾ (17:8), meaning: We sent them so that they would distress your faces.

Allah says: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: to divert us. It is said: "I turned so-and-so away from such-and-such" when you diverted him. From this comes iltifat (turning, a shift of grammatical person), which is turning away from what you were facing.

Allah says: ﴿And that greatness may be yours in the land﴾. Aban and Zayd related from Ya'qub: "wa-yakūna lakumā" with the ya. Regarding the meaning of "greatness" there are three opinions: First, kingship and nobility, said by Ibn Abbas. Second, obedience, said by al-Dahhak. Third, exaltation, said by Ibn Zayd. Ibn Abbas said: "the land" here is the land of Egypt.

(p-51) Allah says: ﴿every skilled magician﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "bi-kulli sahhārin" with a shadda on the ha and the alif placed after it.

Allah says: ﴿What you have brought is magic﴾. Most readers read "al-siḥru" without a mad, in the form of a statement, and the meaning is: What you brought of ropes and staffs is magic. This is a rejection of their saying of the truth, "This is magic." Its underlying form is: What you brought is the magic. The alif and lam were added because an indefinite noun, when repeated, becomes definite, as when you say: "I saw a man, and the man spoke to me." Mujahid, Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far, Aban from Asim, and Abu Hatim from Ya'qub read "ālsiḥru" with an extended alif, as an interrogative. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: What is it that you have brought? Is it magic? As a form of rebuke to them. Ibn al-Anbari said: This interrogative means the magnification of magic, not a real question about something unknown, like a person's saying of a mistake he finds grave: "Is this a mistake?", meaning it is of great magnitude as a mistake. The Arabs ask about what is already known to them. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Has my love for you deceived you, that it would kill me, and that whatever you command the heart, it will obey?"

Qays ibn Dhurayh said:

"Will our former days in Dhu al-Talh return, O Lubna, or is there no return for them?"

He asked, though he knew they would not return.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah will nullify it﴾, meaning He will destroy it and expose your deceit. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not allow the work of corrupters to prosper﴾, meaning He does not make their work beneficial to them. ﴿And Allah will establish the truth by His words﴾, meaning He will make it manifest and firmly established, by what He has previously promised of that.
