The one addressing him with this was Jibril (Gabriel). It has come in a hadith that Jibril began stuffing mud into Pharaoh's mouth, fearing that he would be forgiven.

Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said: Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus (peace be upon him) was a righteous servant who used to remember Allah. When he fell into the belly of the fish he asked Allah, and Allah said: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143]. Pharaoh, however, was a tyrannical servant, forgetful of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. So when drowning overtook him he said, "I believe," and Allah said: ﴿Now, when you had disobeyed before?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So today We shall save you﴾. Ya'qub read *nunjīka* (نُنْجِيكَ) with a lightened form. The philologists, including Yunus and Abu 'Ubaydah, said: *nulqīka* ("We shall cast you") upon a *najwah* (نَجْوَة) of the earth, meaning an elevation, so that it would be a sign that he had drowned. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *nunahhīka* (نُنَحِّيكَ) with a *ha'*.

Regarding the reason he was brought out of the sea after drowning, there are three opinions:

First: When Musa and his companions had departed, those among Pharaoh's people who remained in the cities said: "Pharaoh was not drowned; rather, he and his companions are hunting game on the islands of the sea." So Allah revealed to the sea: "Cast Pharaoh out naked," and it was a rescue for a lesson. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to (p-61) the sea: "Cast out what is in you," and the sea threw them up onto the shore. The sea had never cast out a drowned person, and from then on it would not accept a drowned person until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Dahhak reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: The companions of Musa said: "We fear that Pharaoh has not drowned, and we do not believe in his destruction." So Musa called upon his Lord, and He brought him out until they were certain of his destruction. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Qays ibn 'Ubad, 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad, al-Suddi and Muqatil also held this view. Al-Suddi said: When the Children of Israel said, "Pharaoh has not drowned," Musa called upon Allah, and Pharaoh came out with six hundred and twenty thousand men, wearing iron armour, and the Children of Israel seized him and mutilated him. Others mentioned that he was brought out of the sea alone, without his companions.

Ibn Juraij said: Some of the Children of Israel denied his drowning, so the sea cast him onto the shore until the Children of Israel saw him: short, red, as if he were a bull. Abu Sulayman said: The Children of Israel recognised him by a coat of mail he had, made of pearls, the like of which no one else had. As for his face, the wrath of Allah, the Exalted, had changed it.

Third: He used to claim that he was a lord, and a people worshipped him. So Allah, the Exalted, made his affair clear: He drowned him and his companions, then brought him out from among them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His saying: ﴿with your body﴾, there are four opinions:
First: With your body without a soul, said by Mujahid. The mention of "body" is evidence of the absence of the spirit.
Second: With your armour, said by Abu Sakhr. We have already mentioned that he had a coat of mail of pearls, and it was also said of gold, so he was recognised by his armour.
Third: "We shall cast you naked," said by al-Zajjaj.
Fourth: "We shall save you alone," said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿so that you may be a sign to those after you﴾, there are three opinions:
First: So that you may be a sign for those after you as a deterrent, lest they say the same as you said, for if you were a god you would not have drowned. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "after you" (*khalfaka*, خَلْفَكَ) means "behind you," and *āyah* (آيَة) means a sign.

(p-62) Second: So that you may be a sign to the Children of Israel. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: So that you may be a sign to those of his people who had stayed behind, since they had denied his drowning, as we mentioned at the beginning of the verse. Two views are given on the meaning of *āyah* here: one, that it is a lesson for people; the other, that it is a sign indicating his drowning. Al-Zajjaj said: The sign is that he used to claim he was a lord, and his affair became manifest, and he was brought out from among his companions after they had drowned.

Ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' read *liman khalaqaka* (لِمَن خَلَقَكَ) with a *qaf*, meaning "for those who created you."

(p-52) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿None believed in Moses except a few of his people﴾. There are three views on what is meant by "dhurriyyah" here. The first is that it means "a few": this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, whose fathers had died over the long passage of time, and they themselves believed. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: they are those who grew up with Moses when Pharaoh stopped slaughtering the boys. Ibn al-Anbari said: these people were called "dhurriyyah" because they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, even though they had reached maturity.

The third is that they were a people whose mothers were from the Children of Israel and whose fathers were from the Copts. This is the view of Muqatil, and al-Farra' preferred it. He said: they were called "dhurriyyah" just as the children of the Persians were called "al-abna'" (sons), because their mothers were not of the same kind as their fathers.

(p-53) As for the pronoun in "qawmihi" (his people), there are two views. The first is that it refers to Moses; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it refers to Pharaoh; this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

According to the first view, His saying ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾ means "and the chiefs of Pharaoh." Al-Farra' said: He said "wa mala'ihim" (and their chiefs) in the plural, although Pharaoh is singular, because when a king is mentioned, the mind goes to him and to those with him. You say: "The caliph arrived and the people became many," meaning "and those with him." It is also possible that by Pharaoh is meant the family of Pharaoh, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82).

According to the second view, the mention of the chiefs refers to the dhurriyyah. Ibn Jarir said: this is more correct, because among the dhurriyyah there were those whose father was a Copt and whose mother was from the Children of Israel, so he was with Pharaoh against Moses.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿lest he persecute them﴾: "he" means Pharaoh, and he did not say "lest they persecute them," because his people followed the religion of their ruler. There are two views on this persecution. The first is that it is killing; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it is torture; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was overbearing in the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the transgressors﴾: when he was a servant, he claimed lordship.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him﴾. When the Children of Israel complained to Moses about what Pharaoh threatened them with, namely slaughtering their sons and sparing their women, he said this to them.

Regarding His saying ﴿Do not make us a trial﴾ there are three views.

(p-54) The first: do not destroy us with a punishment at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people would say: "If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished, nor would we have been given power over them."

The second: do not give them power over us, so that they will tempt us. Both views were narrated from Mujahid.

The third: do not give them power over us, so that they will be tempted by us, thinking that they are upon the truth. This was said by Abu al-Duha and Abu Mijlaz.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The commentators said: when Moses was sent, Pharaoh ordered the mosques of the Children of Israel to be destroyed, all of them, and they were prevented from prayer. They used to pray only in churches, so they were commanded to take mosques in their houses and pray in them out of fear of Pharaoh. "Tabawwa'a" means "take," and we have explained it in (al-A'raf 7:74). There are two views on what is meant by "Egypt": the first is that it is the well-known country of Egypt; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that it is Alexandria; this was said by Mujahid. There are two views on "houses": the first is that they are mosques; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that they are palaces; this was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾ there are four views.

The first: make them mosques. This was narrated by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd also said so. We have mentioned that Pharaoh ordered their mosques to be demolished, so they were told: make your houses a qiblah instead of the mosques.

The second: make them facing the qiblah. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: facing Mecca. Mujahid said: they were commanded to make them face the Ka'bah, and Muqatil, Qatadah and al-Farra' said the same.

(p-55) The third: make them face one another. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so.

The fourth: make your houses which are in Syria a qiblah for you in prayer, for it is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

If it is asked: "houses" is plural, so how did He say "qiblah" in the singular? Ibn al-Anbari answered this. He said: whoever says the intended qiblah is the Ka'bah, the qiblah was made singular because the Ka'bah is one. He said: it is also possible that He meant: "make your houses qiblas," and He suffices with the singular instead of the plural, as al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"We said: submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts have been cleansed of rancour."

He means: "for we are your brothers." It is also possible that "qiblah" was made singular because it was treated as a verbal noun, so the meaning is: make your houses a turning towards Allah and an intention, since you used it in mosques. It is also possible that it was made singular, and the meaning is: make your houses a thing that is a qiblah, a place that is a qiblah, and a locality that is a qiblah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: complete the prayer. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, O Muhammad. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: give them good tidings of victory in this world and of Paradise in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they had, from the edge of the tent of Egypt to the land of Abyssinia, mountains containing mines of gold, silver, chrysolite and ruby.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾. Regarding the lam in "liyudillu" (so that they may lead astray) there are four views.

The first: it is the lam of "kay" (in order that), and the meaning is: You gave them that in order that they might lead astray. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: it is the lam of consequence, and the meaning is: You gave them that, and it led them to misguidance. Similar is His saying: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8), meaning: their affair ended with it becoming an enemy to them, not that they intended that. This is like saying to one who earned wealth and it led him to destruction: "So-and-so earned his own destruction," though he did not earn the wealth seeking destruction. And they recited:

"For death, every nursing mother raises [her child], and for ruin, people build up [their] life."

Another said:

"For death the mothers nourish their young, just as houses are built for their ruin."

Another said:

"If death has destroyed them, then to death is what the mother bears."

He meant: the outcome of the matter and its end is toward that. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is the lam of supplication, and the meaning is: "Our Lord, test them with misguidance from Your way." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: it is the lam of purpose (li-ajl), and the meaning is: You gave them for the sake of their misguidance, as a punishment from You upon them. Similar is His saying: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:95), meaning: for the sake of your turning away. Some commentators related this.

The people of Kufa, except al-Mufaddal, Zayd, and Abu Hatim on the authority of Ya'qub, recited "liyudillu" with a damma on the ya', meaning: that they may lead others astray.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate﴾. Al-Halabi narrated from 'Abd al-Warith: "utmus" with a damma on the mim, "over their wealth." Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was turned into stone. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Farra' also said so. Al-Qurazi said: He turned their sugar into stone. Ibn Zayd said: their gold, their dirhams, their lentils, and everything they owned became stone. Mujahid said: Allah transformed the palm trees, the fruits and the foods into stone, and this was one of the nine signs. Al-Zajjaj said: obliterating a thing is removing it from its form and the benefit of it in the state it was in originally.

(p-57) The second: they were destroyed, so the meaning is: He destroyed their wealth. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah also said so. From this one says: "his eye was obliterated," meaning it went away, and "the road was obliterated" when it became effaced and worn out.

Regarding His saying ﴿and harden their hearts﴾ there are four views.

The first: seal them. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj also said so.

The second: destroy them as disbelievers. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said so.

The third: "shdud 'alayha" (tighten upon them) with misguidance. Mujahid said this.

The fourth: its meaning is: harden their hearts. Ibn Qutaybah said this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they will not believe﴾. There are two views on this.

The first: it is also a supplication against them, as if he said: "O Allah, so that they will not believe." This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is "so they did not believe." al-A'sha said:

"So let there not expand between your eyes what has been contracted, and do not meet me except with your nose in the dust."

Its meaning: "it did not expand, nor did you meet me."

The second: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾, so the meaning is: You gave them so that they might lead astray, so that they will not believe. Al-Zajjaj related this from al-Mubarrad.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is drowning. Moses was supplicating and Aaron was saying "Amin," and (p-58) Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Your supplication has been answered, so go straight﴾, and between the supplication and the answer there were forty years.

If it is asked: how did He say "your supplication" (du'watukuma) when they were two supplications? There are three answers to this.

The first: the word "da'wah" (supplication) applies to two supplications, and to many supplications, and to a lengthy speech, as we explained in (al-A'raf 7:158) that "kalimah" (word) applies to words. The poet said:

"He made one supplication to his people: 'Come, for your affair has been cut off.'"

So he applied "da'wah" to the expressions that he explained at the end of his verse.

The second: the meaning is: "your supplications have been answered," and he suffices with the singular for the mention of the whole. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two answers. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from 'Asim that he recited "da'awatukuma" with an alif and a fatha on the 'ayn.

The third: Moses was the one who supplicated, so the supplication belonged to him, but when Aaron said "Amin," they were combined in the supplication, because saying "Amin" to a supplication is a part of it.

Regarding His saying ﴿so go straight﴾ there are four views.

The first: go straight in the message and in what I commanded you. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: go straight in calling Pharaoh and his people to obey Allah. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The third: go straight in your supplication against Pharaoh and his people.

The fourth: go straight upon my religion. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned both of these last two views.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾. Most readers recited "tattabi'anni" with a shaddah on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir recited it with it lightened, while all agreed on the shaddah on the nun of "tattabi'anni," except that the heavy nun entered for prohibition as an emphasis, and it was given a kasrah because it was preceded by a sukun and followed by a sukun (of the other nun). The kasrah was chosen for it because it came after an alif, so it was likened to the nun of the dual. Abu 'Ali said: whoever lowers the nun (with kasrah) may have lightened the heavy nun. If you wish, it is in the form of a report while the meaning is a command, like His saying ﴿let them wait by themselves﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:228, 234) and ﴿let no mother be harmed﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:233), meaning: that should not be. If you wish, make it a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying "fastaqima" (go straight), its estimate being: go straight without following.

Regarding "the way of those who do not know" there are two views. The first: they are Pharaoh and his people; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: those who hasten the judgment before its coming; this was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Moses to supplicate against his people?

The answer: some of them say that this was by revelation, and this is a sound view, because it is not supposed of a prophet that he would undertake such a thing except by permission from Allah, mighty and majestic, since his supplication is a cause of retribution.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "atba'ahum" and "tabi'ahum" are the same. Ibn Qutaybah said: "atba'ahum" means he overtook them. ﴿in insolence and enmity﴾, meaning: in injustice. Al-Hasan recited "fattaba'ahum" with a shaddah, and likewise they recited "wa 'udduwan" with a damma on the 'ayn.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 83–92 (part 2 of 2)**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that He"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *annahu* (أنَّهُ) with a fatha on the alif. The meaning is *āmantu bi-annahu* ("I believe that He..."). When the preposition was dropped, the verb reached *an* and it took the accusative. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *innahu* (إنَّهُ) with a kasra on the alif, treating it as following an implied verb of saying, as if he had said: "I believe," and then said: "Indeed He..." (This is a *qira'ah*, a canonical mode of Qur'anic recitation.)

Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah did not accept his faith at the sight of the punishment.

Ibn al-Anbari said: (p-60) Pharaoh inclined toward repentance when the door of repentance had been closed by the arrival of death and the sight of the angels. So it was said to him: ﴿Now?﴾, meaning: now you repent, when you have squandered repentance at its proper time, ﴿and you were among the corrupters﴾ by calling to the worship of other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The one addressing him with this was Jibril (Gabriel). It has come in a hadith that Jibril began stuffing mud into Pharaoh's mouth, fearing that he would be forgiven.

Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said: Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus (peace be upon him) was a righteous servant who used to remember Allah. When he fell into the belly of the fish he asked Allah, and Allah said: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143]. Pharaoh, however, was a tyrannical servant, forgetful of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. So when drowning overtook him he said, "I believe," and Allah said: ﴿Now, when you had disobeyed before?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So today We shall save you﴾. Ya'qub read *nunjīka* (نُنْجِيكَ) with a lightened form. The philologists, including Yunus and Abu 'Ubaydah, said: *nulqīka* ("We shall cast you") upon a *najwah* (نَجْوَة) of the earth, meaning an elevation, so that it would be a sign that he had drowned. So Allah revealed to the sea: "Cast Pharaoh out naked," and it was a rescue for a lesson. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to (p-61) the sea: "Cast out what is in you," and the sea threw them up onto the shore. The sea had never cast out a drowned person, and from then on it would not accept a drowned person until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Dahhak reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: The companions of Musa said: "We fear that Pharaoh has not drowned, and we do not believe in his destruction." So Musa called upon his Lord, and He brought him out until they were certain of his destruction. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Qays ibn 'Ubad, 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad, al-Suddi and Muqatil also held this view. Al-Suddi said: When the Children of Israel said, "Pharaoh has not drowned," Musa called upon Allah, and Pharaoh came out with six hundred and twenty thousand men, wearing iron armour, and the Children of Israel seized him and mutilated him. Others mentioned that he was brought out of the sea alone, without his companions.

Ibn Juraij said: Some of the Children of Israel denied his drowning, so the sea cast him onto the shore until the Children of Israel saw him: short, red, as if he were a bull. Abu Sulayman said: The Children of Israel recognised him by a coat of mail he had, made of pearls, the like of which no one else had. As for his face, the wrath of Allah, the Exalted, had changed it.

Third: He used to claim that he was a lord, and a people worshipped him. So Allah, the Exalted, made his affair clear: He drowned him and his companions, then brought him out from among them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His saying: ﴿with your body﴾, there are four opinions:
First: With your body without a soul, said by Mujahid. The mention of "body" is evidence of the absence of the spirit.
Second: With your armour, said by Abu Sakhr. We have already mentioned that he had a coat of mail of pearls, and it was also said of gold, so he was recognised by his armour.
Third: "We shall cast you naked," said by al-Zajjaj.
Fourth: "We shall save you alone," said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿so that you may be a sign to those after you﴾, there are three opinions:
First: So that you may be a sign for those after you as a deterrent, lest they say the same as you said, for if you were a god you would not have drowned. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "after you" (*khalfaka*, خَلْفَكَ) means "behind you," and *āyah* (آيَة) means a sign.

(p-62) Second: So that you may be a sign to the Children of Israel. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: So that you may be a sign to those of his people who had stayed behind, since they had denied his drowning, as we mentioned at the beginning of the verse. Two views are given on the meaning of *āyah* here: one, that it is a lesson for people; the other, that it is a sign indicating his drowning. Al-Zajjaj said: The sign is that he used to claim he was a lord, and his affair became manifest, and he was brought out from among his companions after they had drowned.

Ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' read *liman khalaqaka* (لِمَن خَلَقَكَ) with a *qaf*, meaning "for those who created you."

(p-52) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿None believed in Moses except a few of his people﴾. There are three views on what is meant by "dhurriyyah" here. The first is that it means "a few": this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, whose fathers had died over the long passage of time, and they themselves believed. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: they are those who grew up with Moses when Pharaoh stopped slaughtering the boys. According to the first view, His saying ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾ means "and the chiefs of Pharaoh." Al-Farra' said: He said "wa mala'ihim" (and their chiefs) in the plural, although Pharaoh is singular, because when a king is mentioned, the mind goes to him and to those with him. You say: "The caliph arrived and the people became many," meaning "and those with him." It is also possible that by Pharaoh is meant the family of Pharaoh, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82).

According to the second view, the mention of the chiefs refers to the dhurriyyah. Ibn Jarir said: this is more correct, because among the dhurriyyah there were those whose father was a Copt and whose mother was from the Children of Israel, so he was with Pharaoh against Moses.

There are two views on this persecution. The first is that it is killing; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it is torture; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was overbearing in the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the transgressors﴾: when he was a servant, he claimed lordship.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him﴾. When the Children of Israel complained to Moses about what Pharaoh threatened them with, namely slaughtering their sons and sparing their women, he said this to them.

Regarding His saying ﴿Do not make us a trial﴾ there are three views.

(p-54) The first: do not destroy us with a punishment at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people would say: "If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished, nor would we have been given power over them."

The second: do not give them power over us, so that they will tempt us. Both views were narrated from Mujahid.

The third: do not give them power over us, so that they will be tempted by us, thinking that they are upon the truth. This was said by Abu al-Duha and Abu Mijlaz.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The commentators said: when Moses was sent, Pharaoh ordered the mosques of the Children of Israel to be destroyed, all of them, and they were prevented from prayer. They used to pray only in churches, so they were commanded to take mosques in their houses and pray in them out of fear of Pharaoh. "Tabawwa'a" means "take," and we have explained it in (al-A'raf 7:74). There are two views on what is meant by "Egypt": the first is that it is the well-known country of Egypt; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that it is Alexandria; this was said by Mujahid. There are two views on "houses": the first is that they are mosques; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that they are palaces; this was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾ there are four views.

The first: make them mosques. This was narrated by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd also said so. We have mentioned that Pharaoh ordered their mosques to be demolished, so they were told: make your houses a qiblah instead of the mosques.

The second: make them facing the qiblah. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: facing Mecca. Mujahid said: they were commanded to make them face the Ka'bah, and Muqatil, Qatadah and al-Farra' said the same.

(p-55) The third: make them face one another. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so.

The fourth: make your houses which are in Syria a qiblah for you in prayer, for it is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

If it is asked: "houses" is plural, so how did He say "qiblah" in the singular? Ibn al-Anbari answered this. He said: whoever says the intended qiblah is the Ka'bah, the qiblah was made singular because the Ka'bah is one. He said: it is also possible that He meant: "make your houses qiblas," and He suffices with the singular instead of the plural, as al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"We said: submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts have been cleansed of rancour."

He means: "for we are your brothers." It is also possible that "qiblah" was made singular because it was treated as a verbal noun, so the meaning is: make your houses a turning towards Allah and an intention, since you used it in mosques. It is also possible that it was made singular, and the meaning is: make your houses a thing that is a qiblah, a place that is a qiblah, and a locality that is a qiblah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: complete the prayer. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, O Muhammad. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: give them good tidings of victory in this world and of Paradise in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they had, from the edge of the tent of Egypt to the land of Abyssinia, mountains containing mines of gold, silver, chrysolite and ruby.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾. Regarding the lam in "liyudillu" (so that they may lead astray) there are four views.

The first: it is the lam of "kay" (in order that), and the meaning is: You gave them that in order that they might lead astray. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: it is the lam of consequence, and the meaning is: You gave them that, and it led them to misguidance. Similar is His saying: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8), meaning: their affair ended with it becoming an enemy to them, not that they intended that. This is like saying to one who earned wealth and it led him to destruction: "So-and-so earned his own destruction," though he did not earn the wealth seeking destruction. And they recited:

"For death, every nursing mother raises [her child], and for ruin, people build up [their] life."

Another said:

"For death the mothers nourish their young, just as houses are built for their ruin."

Another said:

"If death has destroyed them, then to death is what the mother bears."

He meant: the outcome of the matter and its end is toward that. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is the lam of supplication, and the meaning is: "Our Lord, test them with misguidance from Your way." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: it is the lam of purpose (li-ajl), and the meaning is: You gave them for the sake of their misguidance, as a punishment from You upon them. Similar is His saying: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:95), meaning: for the sake of your turning away. Some commentators related this.

The people of Kufa, except al-Mufaddal, Zayd, and Abu Hatim on the authority of Ya'qub, recited "liyudillu" with a damma on the ya', meaning: that they may lead others astray.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate﴾. Al-Halabi narrated from 'Abd al-Warith: "utmus" with a damma on the mim, "over their wealth." Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was turned into stone. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Farra' also said so. Al-Qurazi said: He turned their sugar into stone. Ibn Zayd said: their gold, their dirhams, their lentils, and everything they owned became stone. Mujahid said: Allah transformed the palm trees, the fruits and the foods into stone, and this was one of the nine signs. Al-Zajjaj said: obliterating a thing is removing it from its form and the benefit of it in the state it was in originally.

(p-57) The second: they were destroyed, so the meaning is: He destroyed their wealth. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah also said so. From this one says: "his eye was obliterated," meaning it went away, and "the road was obliterated" when it became effaced and worn out.

Regarding His saying ﴿and harden their hearts﴾ there are four views.

The first: seal them. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj also said so.

The second: destroy them as disbelievers. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said so.

The third: "shdud 'alayha" (tighten upon them) with misguidance. Mujahid said this.

The fourth: its meaning is: harden their hearts. Ibn Qutaybah said this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they will not believe﴾. There are two views on this.

The first: it is also a supplication against them, as if he said: "O Allah, so that they will not believe." This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is "so they did not believe." al-A'sha said:

"So let there not expand between your eyes what has been contracted, and do not meet me except with your nose in the dust."

Its meaning: "it did not expand, nor did you meet me."

The second: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾, so the meaning is: You gave them so that they might lead astray, so that they will not believe. Al-Zajjaj related this from al-Mubarrad.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is drowning. Moses was supplicating and Aaron was saying "Amin," and (p-58) Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Your supplication has been answered, so go straight﴾, and between the supplication and the answer there were forty years.

If it is asked: how did He say "your supplication" (du'watukuma) when they were two supplications? There are three answers to this.

The first: the word "da'wah" (supplication) applies to two supplications, and to many supplications, and to a lengthy speech, as we explained in (al-A'raf 7:158) that "kalimah" (word) applies to words. The poet said:

"He made one supplication to his people: 'Come, for your affair has been cut off.'"

So he applied "da'wah" to the expressions that he explained at the end of his verse.

The second: the meaning is: "your supplications have been answered," and he suffices with the singular for the mention of the whole. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two answers. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from 'Asim that he recited "da'awatukuma" with an alif and a fatha on the 'ayn.

The third: Moses was the one who supplicated, so the supplication belonged to him, but when Aaron said "Amin," they were combined in the supplication, because saying "Amin" to a supplication is a part of it.

Regarding His saying ﴿so go straight﴾ there are four views.

The first: go straight in the message and in what I commanded you. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: go straight in calling Pharaoh and his people to obey Allah. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The third: go straight in your supplication against Pharaoh and his people.

The fourth: go straight upon my religion. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned both of these last two views.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾. Most readers recited "tattabi'anni" with a shaddah on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir recited it with it lightened, while all agreed on the shaddah on the nun of "tattabi'anni," except that the heavy nun entered for prohibition as an emphasis, and it was given a kasrah because it was preceded by a sukun and followed by a sukun (of the other nun). The kasrah was chosen for it because it came after an alif, so it was likened to the nun of the dual. Abu 'Ali said: whoever lowers the nun (with kasrah) may have lightened the heavy nun. If you wish, it is in the form of a report while the meaning is a command, like His saying ﴿let them wait by themselves﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:228, 234) and ﴿let no mother be harmed﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:233), meaning: that should not be. If you wish, make it a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying "fastaqima" (go straight), its estimate being: go straight without following.

Regarding "the way of those who do not know" there are two views. The first: they are Pharaoh and his people; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: those who hasten the judgment before its coming; this was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Moses to supplicate against his people?

The answer: some of them say that this was by revelation, and this is a sound view, because it is not supposed of a prophet that he would undertake such a thing except by permission from Allah, mighty and majestic, since his supplication is a cause of retribution.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "atba'ahum" and "tabi'ahum" are the same. Ibn Qutaybah said: "atba'ahum" means he overtook them. ﴿in insolence and enmity﴾, meaning: in injustice. Al-Hasan recited "fattaba'ahum" with a shaddah, and likewise they recited "wa 'udduwan" with a damma on the 'ayn.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 83–92 (part 2 of 2)**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that He"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *annahu* (أنَّهُ) with a fatha on the alif. The meaning is *āmantu bi-annahu* ("I believe that He..."). When the preposition was dropped, the verb reached *an* and it took the accusative. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *innahu* (إنَّهُ) with a kasra on the alif, treating it as following an implied verb of saying, as if he had said: "I believe," and then said: "Indeed He..." (This is a *qira'ah*, a canonical mode of Qur'anic recitation.)

Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah did not accept his faith at the sight of the punishment.

Ibn al-Anbari said: (p-60) Pharaoh inclined toward repentance when the door of repentance had been closed by the arrival of death and the sight of the angels. So it was said to him: ﴿Now?﴾, meaning: now you repent, when you have squandered repentance at its proper time, ﴿and you were among the corrupters﴾ by calling to the worship of other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The one addressing him with this was Jibril (Gabriel). It has come in a hadith that Jibril began stuffing mud into Pharaoh's mouth, fearing that he would be forgiven.

Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said: Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus (peace be upon him) was a righteous servant who used to remember Allah. When he fell into the belly of the fish he asked Allah, and Allah said: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143]. Pharaoh, however, was a tyrannical servant, forgetful of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. So when drowning overtook him he said, "I believe," and Allah said: ﴿Now, when you had disobeyed before?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So today We shall save you﴾. Ya'qub read *nunjīka* (نُنْجِيكَ) with a lightened form. The philologists, including Yunus and Abu 'Ubaydah, said: *nulqīka* ("We shall cast you") upon a *najwah* (نَجْوَة) of the earth, meaning an elevation, so that it would be a sign that he had drowned. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *nunahhīka* (نُنَحِّيكَ) with a *ha'*.

Regarding the reason he was brought out of the sea after drowning, there are three opinions:

First: When Musa and his companions had departed, those among Pharaoh's people who remained in the cities said: "Pharaoh was not drowned; rather, he and his companions are hunting game on the islands of the sea." So Allah revealed to the sea: "Cast Pharaoh out naked," and it was a rescue for a lesson. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to (p-61) the sea: "Cast out what is in you," and the sea threw them up onto the shore. The sea had never cast out a drowned person, and from then on it would not accept a drowned person until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Dahhak reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: The companions of Musa said: "We fear that Pharaoh has not drowned, and we do not believe in his destruction." So Musa called upon his Lord, and He brought him out until they were certain of his destruction. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Qays ibn 'Ubad, 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad, al-Suddi and Muqatil also held this view. Al-Suddi said: When the Children of Israel said, "Pharaoh has not drowned," Musa called upon Allah, and Pharaoh came out with six hundred and twenty thousand men, wearing iron armour, and the Children of Israel seized him and mutilated him. Others mentioned that he was brought out of the sea alone, without his companions.

Ibn Juraij said: Some of the Children of Israel denied his drowning, so the sea cast him onto the shore until the Children of Israel saw him: short, red, as if he were a bull. Abu Sulayman said: The Children of Israel recognised him by a coat of mail he had, made of pearls, the like of which no one else had. As for his face, the wrath of Allah, the Exalted, had changed it.

Third: He used to claim that he was a lord, and a people worshipped him. So Allah, the Exalted, made his affair clear: He drowned him and his companions, then brought him out from among them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His saying: ﴿with your body﴾, there are four opinions:
First: With your body without a soul, said by Mujahid. The mention of "body" is evidence of the absence of the spirit.
Second: With your armour, said by Abu Sakhr. We have already mentioned that he had a coat of mail of pearls, and it was also said of gold, so he was recognised by his armour.
Third: "We shall cast you naked," said by al-Zajjaj.
Fourth: "We shall save you alone," said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿so that you may be a sign to those after you﴾, there are three opinions:
First: So that you may be a sign for those after you as a deterrent, lest they say the same as you said, for if you were a god you would not have drowned. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "after you" (*khalfaka*, خَلْفَكَ) means "behind you," and *āyah* (آيَة) means a sign.

(p-62) Second: So that you may be a sign to the Children of Israel. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: So that you may be a sign to those of his people who had stayed behind, since they had denied his drowning, as we mentioned at the beginning of the verse. Two views are given on the meaning of *āyah* here: one, that it is a lesson for people; the other, that it is a sign indicating his drowning. Al-Zajjaj said: The sign is that he used to claim he was a lord, and his affair became manifest, and he was brought out from among his companions after they had drowned.

Ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' read *liman khalaqaka* (لِمَن خَلَقَكَ) with a *qaf*, meaning "for those who created you."

(p-52) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿None believed in Moses except a few of his people﴾. There are three views on what is meant by "dhurriyyah" here. The first is that it means "a few": this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, whose fathers had died over the long passage of time, and they themselves believed. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: they are those who grew up with Moses when Pharaoh stopped slaughtering the boys. Ibn al-Anbari said: these people were called "dhurriyyah" because they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, even though they had reached maturity.

The third is that they were a people whose mothers were from the Children of Israel and whose fathers were from the Copts. This is the view of Muqatil, and al-Farra' preferred it. He said: they were called "dhurriyyah" just as the children of the Persians were called "al-abna'" (sons), because their mothers were not of the same kind as their fathers.

(p-53) As for the pronoun in "qawmihi" (his people), there are two views. The first is that it refers to Moses; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it refers to Pharaoh; this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

According to the first view, His saying ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾ means "and the chiefs of Pharaoh." Al-Farra' said: He said "wa mala'ihim" (and their chiefs) in the plural, although Pharaoh is singular, because when a king is mentioned, the mind goes to him and to those with him. You say: "The caliph arrived and the people became many," meaning "and those with him." It is also possible that by Pharaoh is meant the family of Pharaoh, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82).

According to the second view, the mention of the chiefs refers to the dhurriyyah. Ibn Jarir said: this is more correct, because among the dhurriyyah there were those whose father was a Copt and whose mother was from the Children of Israel, so he was with Pharaoh against Moses.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿lest he persecute them﴾: "he" means Pharaoh, and he did not say "lest they persecute them," because his people followed the religion of their ruler. There are two views on this persecution. The first is that it is killing; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it is torture; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was overbearing in the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the transgressors﴾: when he was a servant, he claimed lordship.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him﴾. When the Children of Israel complained to Moses about what Pharaoh threatened them with, namely slaughtering their sons and sparing their women, he said this to them.

Regarding His saying ﴿Do not make us a trial﴾ there are three views.

(p-54) The first: do not destroy us with a punishment at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people would say: "If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished, nor would we have been given power over them."

The second: do not give them power over us, so that they will tempt us. Both views were narrated from Mujahid.

The third: do not give them power over us, so that they will be tempted by us, thinking that they are upon the truth. This was said by Abu al-Duha and Abu Mijlaz.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The commentators said: when Moses was sent, Pharaoh ordered the mosques of the Children of Israel to be destroyed, all of them, and they were prevented from prayer. They used to pray only in churches, so they were commanded to take mosques in their houses and pray in them out of fear of Pharaoh. "Tabawwa'a" means "take," and we have explained it in (al-A'raf 7:74). There are two views on what is meant by "Egypt": the first is that it is the well-known country of Egypt; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that it is Alexandria; this was said by Mujahid. There are two views on "houses": the first is that they are mosques; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that they are palaces; this was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾ there are four views.

The first: make them mosques. This was narrated by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd also said so. We have mentioned that Pharaoh ordered their mosques to be demolished, so they were told: make your houses a qiblah instead of the mosques.

The second: make them facing the qiblah. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: facing Mecca. Mujahid said: they were commanded to make them face the Ka'bah, and Muqatil, Qatadah and al-Farra' said the same.

(p-55) The third: make them face one another. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so.

The fourth: make your houses which are in Syria a qiblah for you in prayer, for it is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

If it is asked: "houses" is plural, so how did He say "qiblah" in the singular? Ibn al-Anbari answered this. He said: whoever says the intended qiblah is the Ka'bah, the qiblah was made singular because the Ka'bah is one. He said: it is also possible that He meant: "make your houses qiblas," and He suffices with the singular instead of the plural, as al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"We said: submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts have been cleansed of rancour."

He means: "for we are your brothers." It is also possible that "qiblah" was made singular because it was treated as a verbal noun, so the meaning is: make your houses a turning towards Allah and an intention, since you used it in mosques. It is also possible that it was made singular, and the meaning is: make your houses a thing that is a qiblah, a place that is a qiblah, and a locality that is a qiblah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: complete the prayer. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, O Muhammad. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: give them good tidings of victory in this world and of Paradise in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they had, from the edge of the tent of Egypt to the land of Abyssinia, mountains containing mines of gold, silver, chrysolite and ruby.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾. Regarding the lam in "liyudillu" (so that they may lead astray) there are four views.

The first: it is the lam of "kay" (in order that), and the meaning is: You gave them that in order that they might lead astray. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: it is the lam of consequence, and the meaning is: You gave them that, and it led them to misguidance. Similar is His saying: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8), meaning: their affair ended with it becoming an enemy to them, not that they intended that. This is like saying to one who earned wealth and it led him to destruction: "So-and-so earned his own destruction," though he did not earn the wealth seeking destruction. And they recited:

"For death, every nursing mother raises [her child], and for ruin, people build up [their] life."

Another said:

"For death the mothers nourish their young, just as houses are built for their ruin."

Another said:

"If death has destroyed them, then to death is what the mother bears."

He meant: the outcome of the matter and its end is toward that. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is the lam of supplication, and the meaning is: "Our Lord, test them with misguidance from Your way." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: it is the lam of purpose (li-ajl), and the meaning is: You gave them for the sake of their misguidance, as a punishment from You upon them. Similar is His saying: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:95), meaning: for the sake of your turning away. Some commentators related this.

The people of Kufa, except al-Mufaddal, Zayd, and Abu Hatim on the authority of Ya'qub, recited "liyudillu" with a damma on the ya', meaning: that they may lead others astray.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate﴾. Al-Halabi narrated from 'Abd al-Warith: "utmus" with a damma on the mim, "over their wealth." Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was turned into stone. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Farra' also said so. Al-Qurazi said: He turned their sugar into stone. Ibn Zayd said: their gold, their dirhams, their lentils, and everything they owned became stone. Mujahid said: Allah transformed the palm trees, the fruits and the foods into stone, and this was one of the nine signs. Al-Zajjaj said: obliterating a thing is removing it from its form and the benefit of it in the state it was in originally.

(p-57) The second: they were destroyed, so the meaning is: He destroyed their wealth. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah also said so. From this one says: "his eye was obliterated," meaning it went away, and "the road was obliterated" when it became effaced and worn out.

Regarding His saying ﴿and harden their hearts﴾ there are four views.

The first: seal them. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj also said so.

The second: destroy them as disbelievers. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said so.

The third: "shdud 'alayha" (tighten upon them) with misguidance. Mujahid said this.

The fourth: its meaning is: harden their hearts. Ibn Qutaybah said this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they will not believe﴾. There are two views on this.

The first: it is also a supplication against them, as if he said: "O Allah, so that they will not believe." This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is "so they did not believe." al-A'sha said:

"So let there not expand between your eyes what has been contracted, and do not meet me except with your nose in the dust."

Its meaning: "it did not expand, nor did you meet me."

The second: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾, so the meaning is: You gave them so that they might lead astray, so that they will not believe. Al-Zajjaj related this from al-Mubarrad.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is drowning. Moses was supplicating and Aaron was saying "Amin," and (p-58) Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Your supplication has been answered, so go straight﴾, and between the supplication and the answer there were forty years.

If it is asked: how did He say "your supplication" (du'watukuma) when they were two supplications? There are three answers to this.

The first: the word "da'wah" (supplication) applies to two supplications, and to many supplications, and to a lengthy speech, as we explained in (al-A'raf 7:158) that "kalimah" (word) applies to words. The poet said:

"He made one supplication to his people: 'Come, for your affair has been cut off.'"

So he applied "da'wah" to the expressions that he explained at the end of his verse.

The second: the meaning is: "your supplications have been answered," and he suffices with the singular for the mention of the whole. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two answers. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from 'Asim that he recited "da'awatukuma" with an alif and a fatha on the 'ayn.

The third: Moses was the one who supplicated, so the supplication belonged to him, but when Aaron said "Amin," they were combined in the supplication, because saying "Amin" to a supplication is a part of it.

Regarding His saying ﴿so go straight﴾ there are four views.

The first: go straight in the message and in what I commanded you. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: go straight in calling Pharaoh and his people to obey Allah. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The third: go straight in your supplication against Pharaoh and his people.

The fourth: go straight upon my religion. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned both of these last two views.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾. Most readers recited "tattabi'anni" with a shaddah on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir recited it with it lightened, while all agreed on the shaddah on the nun of "tattabi'anni," except that the heavy nun entered for prohibition as an emphasis, and it was given a kasrah because it was preceded by a sukun and followed by a sukun (of the other nun). The kasrah was chosen for it because it came after an alif, so it was likened to the nun of the dual. Abu 'Ali said: whoever lowers the nun (with kasrah) may have lightened the heavy nun. If you wish, it is in the form of a report while the meaning is a command, like His saying ﴿let them wait by themselves﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:228, 234) and ﴿let no mother be harmed﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:233), meaning: that should not be. If you wish, make it a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying "fastaqima" (go straight), its estimate being: go straight without following.

Regarding "the way of those who do not know" there are two views. The first: they are Pharaoh and his people; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: those who hasten the judgment before its coming; this was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Moses to supplicate against his people?

The answer: some of them say that this was by revelation, and this is a sound view, because it is not supposed of a prophet that he would undertake such a thing except by permission from Allah, mighty and majestic, since his supplication is a cause of retribution.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "atba'ahum" and "tabi'ahum" are the same. Ibn Qutaybah said: "atba'ahum" means he overtook them. ﴿in insolence and enmity﴾, meaning: in injustice. Al-Hasan recited "fattaba'ahum" with a shaddah, and likewise they recited "wa 'udduwan" with a damma on the 'ayn.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 10, verses 83–92 (part 2 of 2)**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that He"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *annahu* (أنَّهُ) with a fatha on the alif. The meaning is *āmantu bi-annahu* ("I believe that He..."). When the preposition was dropped, the verb reached *an* and it took the accusative. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *innahu* (إنَّهُ) with a kasra on the alif, treating it as following an implied verb of saying, as if he had said: "I believe," and then said: "Indeed He..." (This is a *qira'ah*, a canonical mode of Qur'anic recitation.)

Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah did not accept his faith at the sight of the punishment.

Ibn al-Anbari said: (p-60) Pharaoh inclined toward repentance when the door of repentance had been closed by the arrival of death and the sight of the angels. So it was said to him: ﴿Now?﴾, meaning: now you repent, when you have squandered repentance at its proper time, ﴿and you were among the corrupters﴾ by calling to the worship of other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The one addressing him with this was Jibril (Gabriel). It has come in a hadith that Jibril began stuffing mud into Pharaoh's mouth, fearing that he would be forgiven.

Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said: Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus (peace be upon him) was a righteous servant who used to remember Allah. When he fell into the belly of the fish he asked Allah, and Allah said: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143]. Pharaoh, however, was a tyrannical servant, forgetful of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. So when drowning overtook him he said, "I believe," and Allah said: ﴿Now, when you had disobeyed before?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So today We shall save you﴾. Ya'qub read *nunjīka* (نُنْجِيكَ) with a lightened form. The philologists, including Yunus and Abu 'Ubaydah, said: *nulqīka* ("We shall cast you") upon a *najwah* (نَجْوَة) of the earth, meaning an elevation, so that it would be a sign that he had drowned. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *nunahhīka* (نُنَحِّيكَ) with a *ha'*.

Regarding the reason he was brought out of the sea after drowning, there are three opinions:

First: When Musa and his companions had departed, those among Pharaoh's people who remained in the cities said: "Pharaoh was not drowned; rather, he and his companions are hunting game on the islands of the sea." So Allah revealed to the sea: "Cast Pharaoh out naked," and it was a rescue for a lesson. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to (p-61) the sea: "Cast out what is in you," and the sea threw them up onto the shore. The sea had never cast out a drowned person, and from then on it would not accept a drowned person until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Dahhak reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: The companions of Musa said: "We fear that Pharaoh has not drowned, and we do not believe in his destruction." So Musa called upon his Lord, and He brought him out until they were certain of his destruction. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported this from Ibn 'Abbas. Qays ibn 'Ubad, 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad, al-Suddi and Muqatil also held this view. Al-Suddi said: When the Children of Israel said, "Pharaoh has not drowned," Musa called upon Allah, and Pharaoh came out with six hundred and twenty thousand men, wearing iron armour, and the Children of Israel seized him and mutilated him. Others mentioned that he was brought out of the sea alone, without his companions.

Ibn Juraij said: Some of the Children of Israel denied his drowning, so the sea cast him onto the shore until the Children of Israel saw him: short, red, as if he were a bull. Abu Sulayman said: The Children of Israel recognised him by a coat of mail he had, made of pearls, the like of which no one else had. As for his face, the wrath of Allah, the Exalted, had changed it.

Third: He used to claim that he was a lord, and a people worshipped him. So Allah, the Exalted, made his affair clear: He drowned him and his companions, then brought him out from among them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His saying: ﴿with your body﴾, there are four opinions:
First: With your body without a soul, said by Mujahid. The mention of "body" is evidence of the absence of the spirit.
Second: With your armour, said by Abu Sakhr. We have already mentioned that he had a coat of mail of pearls, and it was also said of gold, so he was recognised by his armour.
Third: "We shall cast you naked," said by al-Zajjaj.
Fourth: "We shall save you alone," said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿so that you may be a sign to those after you﴾, there are three opinions:
First: So that you may be a sign for those after you as a deterrent, lest they say the same as you said, for if you were a god you would not have drowned. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "after you" (*khalfaka*, خَلْفَكَ) means "behind you," and *āyah* (آيَة) means a sign.

(p-62) Second: So that you may be a sign to the Children of Israel. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: So that you may be a sign to those of his people who had stayed behind, since they had denied his drowning, as we mentioned at the beginning of the verse. Two views are given on the meaning of *āyah* here: one, that it is a lesson for people; the other, that it is a sign indicating his drowning. Al-Zajjaj said: The sign is that he used to claim he was a lord, and his affair became manifest, and he was brought out from among his companions after they had drowned.

Ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' read *liman khalaqaka* (لِمَن خَلَقَكَ) with a *qaf*, meaning "for those who created you."

(p-52) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿None believed in Moses except a few of his people﴾. There are three views on what is meant by "dhurriyyah" here. The first is that it means "a few": this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, whose fathers had died over the long passage of time, and they themselves believed. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: they are those who grew up with Moses when Pharaoh stopped slaughtering the boys. Ibn al-Anbari said: these people were called "dhurriyyah" because they were the children of those to whom Moses was sent, even though they had reached maturity.

The third is that they were a people whose mothers were from the Children of Israel and whose fathers were from the Copts. This is the view of Muqatil, and al-Farra' preferred it. He said: they were called "dhurriyyah" just as the children of the Persians were called "al-abna'" (sons), because their mothers were not of the same kind as their fathers.

(p-53) As for the pronoun in "qawmihi" (his people), there are two views. The first is that it refers to Moses; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it refers to Pharaoh; this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

According to the first view, His saying ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾ means "and the chiefs of Pharaoh." Al-Farra' said: He said "wa mala'ihim" (and their chiefs) in the plural, although Pharaoh is singular, because when a king is mentioned, the mind goes to him and to those with him. You say: "The caliph arrived and the people became many," meaning "and those with him." It is also possible that by Pharaoh is meant the family of Pharaoh, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82).

According to the second view, the mention of the chiefs refers to the dhurriyyah. Ibn Jarir said: this is more correct, because among the dhurriyyah there were those whose father was a Copt and whose mother was from the Children of Israel, so he was with Pharaoh against Moses.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿lest he persecute them﴾: "he" means Pharaoh, and he did not say "lest they persecute them," because his people followed the religion of their ruler. There are two views on this persecution. The first is that it is killing; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it is torture; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was overbearing in the land of Egypt. ﴿And indeed he was among the transgressors﴾: when he was a servant, he claimed lordship.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him﴾. When the Children of Israel complained to Moses about what Pharaoh threatened them with, namely slaughtering their sons and sparing their women, he said this to them.

Regarding His saying ﴿Do not make us a trial﴾ there are three views.

(p-54) The first: do not destroy us with a punishment at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people would say: "If they were upon the truth, they would not have been punished, nor would we have been given power over them."

The second: do not give them power over us, so that they will tempt us. Both views were narrated from Mujahid.

The third: do not give them power over us, so that they will be tempted by us, thinking that they are upon the truth. This was said by Abu al-Duha and Abu Mijlaz.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾. The commentators said: when Moses was sent, Pharaoh ordered the mosques of the Children of Israel to be destroyed, all of them, and they were prevented from prayer. They used to pray only in churches, so they were commanded to take mosques in their houses and pray in them out of fear of Pharaoh. "Tabawwa'a" means "take," and we have explained it in (al-A'raf 7:74). There are two views on what is meant by "Egypt": the first is that it is the well-known country of Egypt; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that it is Alexandria; this was said by Mujahid. There are two views on "houses": the first is that they are mosques; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second is that they are palaces; this was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾ there are four views.

The first: make them mosques. This was narrated by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd also said so. We have mentioned that Pharaoh ordered their mosques to be demolished, so they were told: make your houses a qiblah instead of the mosques.

The second: make them facing the qiblah. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: facing Mecca. Mujahid said: they were commanded to make them face the Ka'bah, and Muqatil, Qatadah and al-Farra' said the same.

(p-55) The third: make them face one another. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so.

The fourth: make your houses which are in Syria a qiblah for you in prayer, for it is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

If it is asked: "houses" is plural, so how did He say "qiblah" in the singular? Ibn al-Anbari answered this. He said: whoever says the intended qiblah is the Ka'bah, the qiblah was made singular because the Ka'bah is one. He said: it is also possible that He meant: "make your houses qiblas," and He suffices with the singular instead of the plural, as al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"We said: submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts have been cleansed of rancour."

He means: "for we are your brothers." It is also possible that "qiblah" was made singular because it was treated as a verbal noun, so the meaning is: make your houses a turning towards Allah and an intention, since you used it in mosques. It is also possible that it was made singular, and the meaning is: make your houses a thing that is a qiblah, a place that is a qiblah, and a locality that is a qiblah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: complete the prayer. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, O Muhammad. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: give them good tidings of victory in this world and of Paradise in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they had, from the edge of the tent of Egypt to the land of Abyssinia, mountains containing mines of gold, silver, chrysolite and ruby.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾. Regarding the lam in "liyudillu" (so that they may lead astray) there are four views.

The first: it is the lam of "kay" (in order that), and the meaning is: You gave them that in order that they might lead astray. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: it is the lam of consequence, and the meaning is: You gave them that, and it led them to misguidance. Similar is His saying: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8), meaning: their affair ended with it becoming an enemy to them, not that they intended that. This is like saying to one who earned wealth and it led him to destruction: "So-and-so earned his own destruction," though he did not earn the wealth seeking destruction. And they recited:

"For death, every nursing mother raises [her child], and for ruin, people build up [their] life."

Another said:

"For death the mothers nourish their young, just as houses are built for their ruin."

Another said:

"If death has destroyed them, then to death is what the mother bears."

He meant: the outcome of the matter and its end is toward that. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is the lam of supplication, and the meaning is: "Our Lord, test them with misguidance from Your way." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: it is the lam of purpose (li-ajl), and the meaning is: You gave them for the sake of their misguidance, as a punishment from You upon them. Similar is His saying: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:95), meaning: for the sake of your turning away. Some commentators related this.

The people of Kufa, except al-Mufaddal, Zayd, and Abu Hatim on the authority of Ya'qub, recited "liyudillu" with a damma on the ya', meaning: that they may lead others astray.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate﴾. Al-Halabi narrated from 'Abd al-Warith: "utmus" with a damma on the mim, "over their wealth." Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was turned into stone. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Farra' also said so. Al-Qurazi said: He turned their sugar into stone. Ibn Zayd said: their gold, their dirhams, their lentils, and everything they owned became stone. Mujahid said: Allah transformed the palm trees, the fruits and the foods into stone, and this was one of the nine signs. Al-Zajjaj said: obliterating a thing is removing it from its form and the benefit of it in the state it was in originally.

(p-57) The second: they were destroyed, so the meaning is: He destroyed their wealth. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah also said so. From this one says: "his eye was obliterated," meaning it went away, and "the road was obliterated" when it became effaced and worn out.

The first: seal them. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj also said so.

The second: destroy them as disbelievers. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said so.

The third: "shdud 'alayha" (tighten upon them) with misguidance. Mujahid said this.

The fourth: its meaning is: harden their hearts. Ibn Qutaybah said this.

The first: it is also a supplication against them, as if he said: "O Allah, so that they will not believe." This was said by al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is "so they did not believe." al-A'sha said:

"So let there not expand between your eyes what has been contracted, and do not meet me except with your nose in the dust."

Its meaning: "it did not expand, nor did you meet me."
